The Śivadharma:
Oṃ, salutation to Mahāgaṇapati. Hariḥ Oṃ. May there be no obstacle. Salutation to the venerable Gurus.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva.
May there be auspiciousness at all times for the entire world in every way without exception;
and may there always be auspiciousness for cows, brahmins, and kings.
Auspicious in the beginning, auspicious in the middle, and likewise auspicious in the end—
what could be inauspicious for all devotees of Śiva and his followers?
Nandikeśvara, who is seated comfortably on the summit of Mount Meru, surrounded by hosts of sages,
is the benefactor of the worlds, peaceful, and omniscient.
Rising from among them, the sage Sanatkumāra, the best of Brahmā’s sons and one of great austerity, questioned Vidhi with a smile.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, devoted to the auspicious Dharma,
all these who have assembled here desire to hear the supreme Dharma.
Sacrificial rites such as the Agniṣṭoma and others require great wealth and effort;
they do not yield abundant ultimate fruits and are accompanied by much exertion.
Since they cannot be performed by twice-born men of meager means,
therefore tell me an easy method that accomplishes all desires and goals.
For the welfare of all sentient beings, [I shall proclaim] the eternal Śivadharma,
by which the Siddhas, gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas have attained perfection.
The sages, kinnaras, yakṣas, as well as kiṃpuruṣas and others,
along with various other hosts, were all devoted to the dharma of Śiva.
"By worshipping whom all men become his devotees and followers of the Śiva-dharma?
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
"Listen, I shall describe the easy means which yields great fruit."
The supreme, eternal dharma of auspiciousness among all dharmas.
This was previously told by Śiva to Pārvatī, to Ṣaṇmukha,
to the Gaṇas, to the foremost of the gods, and especially to us.
For all living beings submerged in the ocean of ignorance,
this glorious Śivadharmottara has been proclaimed as a boat for the sake of crossing over.
O Rudras, there is no doubt that this supreme dharma is practiced by those whose minds are tranquil, who are devotees of Śiva, and who seek Śiva.
Whether in a village or in a forest, whether in water or on land—
wherever a *liṅga* is seen, there indeed are all sacred fords (*tīrthas*).
Those who remember Virūpākṣa once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or constantly at all times— they are Rudras; of this there is no doubt.
Those men who shall proclaim [the names] of the Rudras even once, they shall quickly be liberated from all sins, even those committed throughout all their previous births.
Those who always worship Rudra are not merely human beings;
fallen from the world of Rudra, they are Rudras themselves—of this there is no doubt.
That embodied being by whom the Blessed Lord Śiva has not been worshipped wanders for a long time in this cycle of existence, which is an ocean of suffering.
His mind is greatly flawed, and his enjoyment is mute regarding his own welfare,
he who does not contemplate [the Lord] for even a moment, or a muhūrta, or for a single day.
Having attained this human birth which is so difficult to find, those who worship Sadāśiva have indeed made their lives fruitful; they are the best among men, having accomplished their purpose.
But those who are devoted to worldly existence, with minds bowed toward Bhava,
and who are intent on the constant recollection of worldly existence, become partakers of suffering because of that.
Delightful mansions, graceful women adorned with ornaments,
and wealth whose limits are unseen— these are the fruits of the ritual worship of Śiva.
Those who desire great enjoyments or sovereignty in the abode of the thirty gods should always worship the lotus feet of Hara.
For one who worships Śiva, there shall arise good fortune, a beautiful form, a virtuous nature through the power of generosity, valor, and world-wide renown.
One who is not Rudra cannot remember Rudra; one who is not Rudra cannot worship Rudra;
one who is not Rudra cannot glorify Rudra; and one who is not Rudra cannot attain Rudra.
This is the essence of the Śiva-dharma: unwavering devotion to Śiva. And that devotion has been declared by Śiva to have eight limbs; it should be practiced constantly with diligent effort.
The Blessed Lord said: Affection for My devotees, rejoicing in their worship,
personally worshipping Me with devotion, and bodily exertion for My sake;
Devotion in hearing my stories, transformations of voice, eyes, and limbs [due to emotion],
constant remembrance of me, and not depending on anyone other than me.
Even if this eightfold devotion exists in a barbarian,
he is a lord of Brahmins, a venerable sage, one who has conquered his senses, and a true scholar.
One who is learned in the four Vedas is not dear to me; rather, even one who cooks his own food is dear if he is my devotee.
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be accepted, and he is to be honored just as I am.
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—
of him I am never lost, and he is never lost to Me.
The man who, while established in his observance, constantly worships me,
perishes as he searches for me in mountains and difficult terrains.
He who sees me as all-pervading and sees everything as abiding in me—
in him I am eternally established, and he is eternally established in me.
Devotion to Śiva is very difficult to attain; the worship of Śiva is difficult to achieve;
giving gifts to Śiva is very rare, and the fire-oblation to Śiva is hard to find.
The knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to attain, and its practice is exceedingly difficult;
yet even more difficult to find is that which is to be known: the recitation and meditation whose essence is Śiva.
The attainment of these two is extremely difficult; their practice is exceedingly rare.
Knowing this to be very hard to obtain, one should take refuge in devotion to Śiva.
Blessed are those people who have gone for refuge to Śiva;
this constant mindfulness directed toward Śiva is their [path] by day and by night.
The life of that person whose tongue-tip bears the two syllables "Śi-va," joined with salutations and the like, is fruitful.
Thus, this entire Śivadharma has been briefly indicated for you in due order in the first chapter; the detailed exposition of the remainder follows.
Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with devotion,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Dakinis of various forms, rakshasas, and leaders of pretas— none of these, nor indeed other harmful beings, cause him any affliction.
Enemies go to destruction; one is not afflicted by any diseases.
One shall not be oppressed by any diseases, nor shall calamities touch them.
One shall attain wealth, longevity, fame, knowledge, and incomparable power;
endowed with perfect virtues, auspicious things constantly reach their full development.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Devotion," in the glorious Śivadharmaśāstra.
The second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"I desire to hear, in accordance with reality, the complete procedure for the worship of the Liṅga."
O Blessed One, O Nandikeśvara, by your special grace, [may this be so].
Whatever merit is gained from installing a linga, whatever is gained from constructing a temple for Śiva,
the merit gained from sweeping it, and the merit gained from smearing it with unguents;

Whatever merit arises from the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), medicinal herbs, seeds, ritual bathing, auspicious music, the honoring of the venerable, giving gifts, and bathing with water— [all that is attained here].
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or bathing with curd,
whatever merit is gained by bathing with ghee, and whatever results from anointing with ghee— [all that is attained through this].

Whatever merit is gained by bathing with honey and whatever merit is gained by bathing with sugarcane juice, that same merit is obtained by bathing after anointing the body with unguents and by bathing with water containing *kuśa* grass and flowers.
And that which occurs with water containing gold and jewels, with waters of fragrant sandalwood, with water of camphor and agallochum, or with pure water;
Whatever merit may arise from being anointed with unguents, perfumes, and the like,
as well as from the offering of a palm-leaf fan and the offering of a chowrie;
By worshipping with offerings of pearl-flowers, by filling the liṅga with garlands,
and by hanging flower-garlands upon the pavilion of flowers;
Whatever fruit is obtained through special forms of worship and devotion, by offering garlands upon the altar, by various species of flowers, and even by incenses;
and whatever fruit is obtained by the gift of villages, market towns, cities, and entire regions.
And whatever merit or demerit may arise from its protection or its theft;
What merit does one obtain by giving ascetics mere requisites such as food and drink, or by constructing a dwelling for them?

In the same way, when performing their refinement, as well as rising to meet them and saluting them; in the same way, when performing their refinement, as well as rising to meet them and saluting them.
Whatever else there may be that is subtle, yet remains unexplained due to ignorance—
all of that, please tell us out of compassion for your devotees.
Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Śivadharmaśāstra.
The third chapter.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O best of the sons of the Lotus-born One, you are exceedingly devoted to Śiva."
I shall explain everything in its entirety; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Formerly, when the world had perished in a terrible single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had vanished,
there arose a very great dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
"I am the creator; I am the creator; there is no Lord of the world other than me"—thus Brahmā spoke to Hari, and likewise Hari to Brahmā.
For the purpose of removing the pride of those two gods and for their awakening,
a supreme, fiery Liṅga of Īśvara appeared between them.
Enveloped in garlands of flames, divine, immeasurable, and incomparable,
it stood ten thousand yojanas wide upon those pure waters.
Deluded by the flames of that liṅga, those two best of gods, the lords of the immortals,
were then struck with wonder as they gazed upon it.
Having deliberated with one another regarding his upward and downward movements,
Viṣṇu went below for the sake of discovery, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) went above.
Not seeing him either below or above, the two approached each other and,
with palms joined in reverence, then offered praise to the Liṅga.
O beginningless Lord of the gods, Lord of the lords of knowledge, Great Lord!
O omniscient one, who bestows both theoretical and realized knowledge—salutations be unto You alone.
O you of many forms and great form, supreme among all forms,
who have transcended the ocean of bonds that bind the individual soul, O bestower of boons, homage be to you!
O you whose nature is pure, whose enjoyment is all-pervading, Great Lord;
O Yoga, O Yogin, O Mahāyogin, O Lord of Yoga, homage be to you!
O stainless one, O supportless one, O self-supported one, O untroubled one;
salutations to You, the gracious Supreme Lord, the Master of Yoga.
We two have been deluded by the fickleness of our tongues and have uttered praises; therefore, you should forgive us. One who is not like a boat cannot praise the ocean of your virtues.
That virtuous man who constantly hears this meritorious hymn to the origin of the *liṅga* is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
In the midst of the linga, the supreme linga, measuring a span, stood there;
endowed with meditative absorption and hymns of praise, they beheld it as being of the nature of Śiva.
This is neither gold, nor silver, nor copper, nor crystal, nor pearl;
it exists as a mere hundred thousand [units], peaceful, absolute, and of the nature of Śiva.
Mahādeva, pleased with them both, granted an unsurpassed boon;
having authorized their status as the cause, he vanished right there.
With palms joined in reverence, Viṣṇu bowed down, and Brahmā, too, being devoted to the Brahman;
having first worshipped the Liṅga, they both performed their respective duties.
Brahmā always worships the Liṅga with divine, imperishable mantras;
Viṣṇu constantly worships Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
From that time forward, Brahmā and the others, as well as the gods and demons,
and the sages, have worshipped a linga fashioned in imitation of that very one.
The supreme Garuḍa is the body and the liṅga, the primordial field;
that which is the primal splendor of the Lord is the liṅga known by five names.
At the end of the eon, all the deities dissolve into that *liṅga*:
Brahmā dissolves into the south, and Janārdana into the west.
The Gāyatrī, the most excellent among all the Vedas, resides in the heart;
indeed, the Vedas, together with their six auxiliary limbs, their words, and their step-by-step recitations, dissolve into the head.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, dissolves into his belly;
from him, moreover, everything including Brahmā and all that is mobile and immobile is produced again.
They say that space is the *liṅga* and the earth is its pedestal;
it is called the *liṅga* because it is the abode of all beings due to their dissolution therein.
Having thus established the *liṅga*, which is the source of the existence of all gods, everything that has been installed by him becomes worshipped; of this there is no doubt.
Even Brahmā, intent upon the Brahman, sent forth Viṣṇu with palms joined in reverence;
Brahmā constantly worships the auspicious linga made of stone.
By worshipping it, he attained the supreme state of Brahmahood;
Śakra, the lord of the gods, also [worshipped] the auspicious linga made of jewels.
By worshipping it constantly with devotion, he attained the status of Śakra;
Dhanada always worships that beautiful linga made of gold.
By that [act], the god Dhanada attained the status of the Giver of Wealth;
and the high-souled Viśvedevas [worshipped] a beautiful silver liṅga.
They worship according to the rules with devotion, and through that they have attained the state of being the universe;
Vāyu constantly worships a linga made of brass.
Through that, he attained the state of Vāyu, which brings incomparable qualities;
Viṣṇu always worships this Liṅga made of sapphire.
By that [act], he attained the eternal and singularly wonderful state of Viṣṇu;
the Vasus worship that Liṅga according to the prescribed rites.
For the high-souled ones worship the Aśvins— the terrestrial emblem that brings great prosperity— as the state of the Vasus, according to the prescribed ritual.
Therefore, both of us gods, having assumed divine bodies,
always worship that crystal *vṛddhimat* linga of Varuṇa.
For Varuṇahood has been attained by him, endowed with supernatural power;
Agni, being purified, worships that meritorious linga composed of food.
O Agni, because you have attained that [state] endowed with the form of splendor,
the divine Sun has always worshipped that copper *liṅga* with devotion.
Having attained supreme solar status through constant worship,
Soma always honors the *liṅga* made of pearls.
By that [merit], he too attained the state of Soma, eternally radiant;
the best of serpents worship that manifest linga made of gold.
By that, the Nāgas, rich in excellent enjoyments, shall proceed to the supreme state;
the foremost among the Asuras worship a Liṅga made of black iron.
And those high-souled Rākṣasas of immeasurable prowess,
as well as those Piśācas, worship a linga made of tin and lead.
Endowed with the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), they proceed to the supreme state;
the Guhyakas and others always worship the triple-metal image.
Endowed with the fruits of enjoyment, they go to the abode of the Lord;
the Mothers always worship the Linga made of adamantine metal.
Having attained motherhood, all these go to the supreme state—
so too do the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
They worship Īśāna, the leader of the gods, at all times;
by that, they constantly worship everything established within the liṅga.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should always worship the Liṅga;
for Mahādeva, the Lord, is himself directly established within the Liṅga.
Therefore, for the sake of favoring the worlds, one should worship the Liṅga;
he who, out of delusion, does not worship the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds.
He who constantly worships the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds, is not merely a recipient of heaven, nor of liberation, nor even of sovereignty.
He quickly becomes a vessel for the kingdom of heaven and liberation;
therefore, with a single-minded focus, one should remain committed by vow as long as life lasts.
Even when beset by calamity, the wise always worship Mahādeva;
better indeed is the abandonment of life or even the loss of one's head than [forsaking him].
Having bowed and worshipped the three-eyed Lord, one should eat;
he who thus carries out the worship of Śiva for as long as he lives, [attains his goal].
Longevity, strength, and health—Rudra grants these; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, there is nowhere any merit greater than the worship of the Liṅga.
Having understood this, Sadāśiva—who is saluted by all the gods—should always be worshipped with effort; for he who, out of delusion, hates the Liṅga [is lost].
Even by conversing with him, one may go to hell;
therefore, having thus established the *liṅga* with all effort according to the prescribed ritual, [one should proceed].
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit of merit that one obtains—
the fruit which is found in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas.

A man who installs even a single liṅga according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), shall obtain the fruit of that merit multiplied ten millionfold by installing a permanent liṅga.
One who takes a wife from her mother and father shall obtain merit arising from all desires, multiplied by ten million times ten million.
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, when the dissolution arrives, he [attains liberation].
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated right there;
but if he should desire sovereignty, he is born again in another existence.
He who, having fashioned a linga of earth, worships it according to the Vedic rite, shall become the sovereign of the earth with its seven continents and oceans.
In this very world he becomes wealthy and glorious, and at the end he is born as Rudra;
he who worships the Liṅga during the twilight, having fashioned it from clay with an image.
Listen to the fruit of his merit up to the tenth and eleventh [day]:
with this very body, he wanders upon the earth as Rudra.
The destroyer of the sins of all mortals even by sight or touch,
having uplifted [them], he establishes twenty-one generations in heaven.
He who worships a liṅga made of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, adorned with all kinds of fragrances, rejoices eternally together with his companions like Rudra in heaven.
With fragrant flowers, various fruits,
as well as foods to be chewed and eaten, and drinks, along with ghee lamps,
the wise man should place agarwood on its right side.
One should give a beautiful woman of pleasant character in the western part;
one should give sandalwood in the north and yellow orpiment in the east.
Having thus performed the extensive ritual according to one's wealth,
one should offer it to Śiva on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I declare the fruit that one who constructs even a single liṅga obtains.
Completely liberated from all evil and freed from all calamities,
having become partless and all-pervading, he shall enter the imperishable Śiva.
Even a man who, while playing in the dust, fashions a linga,
shall obtain at the end of his life a kingdom free from rivals and thorns.
Even through a subtle application, one accumulates an immeasurable store of merit.
Since one worships Śiva [through this], therefore one should worship him constantly;
therefore, with every effort, one should listen to it with a purified mind.
Having cast off the cloak of evil, one attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Origin of the Liṅga," in the Śrī Śivadharmaśāstra proclaimed by Nandi.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Nandikeśvara said:
"The devotees of Śiva are possessed of great enthusiasm and are solely intent upon the worship of Śiva."
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, they accomplish all goals.
They endure all dualities with fortitude, their minds are ever-diligent,
they are devoted to helping others, and they take delight in serving their gurus.
They are upright, gentle, pure, compliant, and pleasant of speech;
they are free from pride, wise, and have abandoned rivalry and worldly desire.
They are peaceful, with smiling faces, auspicious, and always welcoming;
they speak little and are not talkative; they are brave and skilled in renunciation.
Endowed with purity of conduct, characterized by compassion and courtesy,
they are free from hypocrisy and envy, and speak only what is truthful.
The wise are devoted to sharing; they are free from deceit and blameless.
They remain unstained by sense objects, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
Even rivers are not turbid, nor do they flow under the sway of anger; those who have cultivated their selves are exceedingly gentle and frequented by the virtuous.
Free from all attachments, the wise do not engage in restless movements with their hands, feet, speech, eyes, ears, head, or bellies.
Having Rudra as their self, devoted to Rudra, portions of Rudra, and spoken of by Rudra—
such are the inhabitants of the earth who become endowed with this conduct.
Resorting to exclusive devotion for the sake of attaining both the supreme and the non-supreme,
one should always worship Śiva while abiding in these qualities.
Maheśvara is the supreme recipient among all worthy recipients;
for he protects one from falling into the ocean of the Dāti hell.
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
whichever vessel arrives, that vessel shall deliver [the donor].
Due to the greatness of that bowl, even a minute gift becomes inexhaustible;
therefore, those who desire immeasurable fruit should always give to him.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, chanted, or presented as worship and oblation to Śiva shall yield absolute results in solitude; of this there is no doubt.
It will yield exclusively and ultimately fruitful results; there is no doubt about this.
One should construct a collection of shrines with devotion, according to one's means.
Whether small or great, the fruit of merit is the same for both the wealthy and the poor.
Whatever a man, though wealthy, may perform with stinginess regarding his wealth,
he— his mind overcome by greed— obtains that very same fruit [of his action].
Therefore, one should set aside one-third of one's wealth for the purpose of livelihood,
and two parts for the sake of dharma, since life is impermanent.
A man who, though possessing little wealth, acts out of devotion, is superior to one who, despite having great riches, does not act because he is devoid of devotion.
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions, if devoid of devotion to Śiva, one would not partake in the merit; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Neither by extremely fierce austerities nor by all the *soma* sacrifices does one go to the divine city of Śiva, except through devotion whose essence is Śiva;
yet he who builds a temple for Śiva out of clay, brick, or stone [attains that goal].
Together with seven times three generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The merit from [an image] made of wood is ten million times that of one made of clay;
the merit from one made of brick is ten million times ten million times that of those made of clay and wood.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the merit in a temple of Śiva increases twofold at each successive stage;
the merit for one made of clay and stone should be known as equal, regardless of whether the patron is wealthy or poor.
Wherever you may go, you should perform meritorious works made of stone or brick;
there, you should construct a temple of Śiva that is new and free from antiquity.
Whoever constructs a temple of Śiva provided with eight bricks,
having shaken off the multitude of his sins, shall also go to the abode of Śiva.
Even one who, while playing, should build a temple for Śiva out of childish impulse,
shall attain a celestial vehicle that travels everywhere in the world of Rudra.
Encircled by divine garlands, adorned with celestial perfumes,
joined with the swaying of swings, and decorated with bells and chowries.
Adorned with a canopy of pearl necklaces, possessing a splendor like that of the sun,
crowded with throngs of Apsarases, and bestowing all desires and happiness.
Having dwelt there for ten million times ten thousand years in happiness with great enjoyments,
he gradually returns to this world and becomes a righteous king.
Seeing and avoiding living beings with a soft and fine broom, one should perform sweeping slowly; thus one obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One should not collect milk from a barren cow that has died due to lack of food, nor should one collect cow dung from cows afflicted by disease or those that have recently given birth.
Having taken cow dung that has settled on its own, or that which has fallen in an auspicious place,
one should discard the uppermost layers repeatedly until it is fresh and free from insects.
He who performs the smearing of the floor with water filtered through a cloth,
while observing and avoiding living beings, shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
He who performs all his duties with water purified by a cloth is a sage, he is a great holy man, he is a yogi, and he shall go to the state of Śiva.
All gifts, sacrifices, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations eventually perish;
but this great gift of fearlessness toward all embodied beings never perishes.
He who performs sweeping and worship continuously for a fortnight is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred crores of yugas.
At its conclusion, he becomes a righteous king, learned in the four Vedas, handsome, pleasing to behold, wealthy, and endowed with all his kinsmen.
Even a person who performs an act in the temple of Śiva through mere association shall attain knowledge after three bodies and obtain peace.
In the realms of the Rudra-devas, someone might attain knowledge;
yet only a rare few on this earth, having attained knowledge, are liberated.
All embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief, as long as they do not become devotees of Śiva.
If even one as inauspicious as this were to have a mind so intensely attached to the sphere of sense objects,
who then would not be liberated from bondage?
Whoever should construct a paved floor resembling the surface of a mirror,
variegated with various colors, or radiant with diverse flowers;
In some places, within the assembly of the temple of Śiva, there were delightful and very smooth areas adorned with lotuses and other flowers, where water-jars had been arranged.
For as many cubits as the ground remains adorned on all sides,
for that many thousands of yugas is one honored in the world of Śiva.
Whoever should plaster a temple of Śiva with white lime using every possible effort shall obtain that much merit as long as the sanctuary remains standing.
The wise man who every year constructs a temple for Śambhu,
whitening it with lime and decorating it beautifully with pigments;
For as many years as one makes that abode of Śiva white,
for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should diligently have paintings executed in the temple of Śiva by those learned in the treatises on painting,
depicting the sports and incarnations of Rudra as proclaimed in the Āgamas.
For as many thousands of yugas as one causes beautiful forms of that very nature to be depicted, for so long one is honored in the world of Rudra; likewise,
he who performs the restoration of a temple of Śiva that is broken or cracked [is similarly rewarded].
Through both the pleasure grove and the dwelling, one obtains the fundamental fruit;
there is no god equal to Rudra, and there is no guru equal to Rudra.
There is no knowledge equal to Rudra’s; there is no austerity equal to Rudra’s.
To him whose body is pure by nature, from whom the mud of impurities has been shaken off.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Gods, whose body and limbs are smeared with white ashes;
salutations to Śarva, the blue-throated one, who is the manifest form of the Unborn.
Salutations to you, who possess many forms, who are beloved, and who are eternal;
salutations to the Supreme, the Great Lord, the seven-limbed, the Great Soul.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Universe, who embodies the aggregate of all past virtues;
who wears the great lord of serpents as a necklace, and who is beautiful with tawny eyes.
Homage be to you, who are rich in diverse deeds and infinite;
to you whose body is bowed by all, yet whose own self is never bowed;
to the one worthy of worship even by those who are themselves worthy of worship; homage to the three-eyed one, the wielder of the trident.

Salutations to you, who are honored by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu; who are the cause of the origin and sustenance [of the world]; who bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; and who are perfectly refined.
Salutations to you, the left-handed one, who possesses a beautiful form, who follows the path of the left, the radiant one, the beloved of the left,
and the Lord of the left.
Whoever shall recite this meritorious and supreme chapter on the temple,
being liberated from all defects, shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Temples, in the glorious Śivadharmaśāstra.
Then the fifth, Nandikeśvara, said: "Of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Lord, whose form is the Liṅga..."
At the time of bathing, one should perform auspicious rites such as the utterance of the word "Victory."
With a trident, conch, vajra, lotus, śrīvatsa, svastika, and so forth,
fashioned from vessels of gold, silver, and the like, and prepared with cow dung and other materials.
One should arrange them beautifully with unbroken grains, sesame seeds, and rice, combined with various colors,
as well as with white mustard seeds mixed with curd.
With *dūrvā* grass, lotuses, lamps, and the like; with the tender shoots of mango, *aśvattha*, and other trees; with pure medicinal herbs; and with all kinds of seeds and sprouts of barley.
On all days beginning with the eighth, as well as during festivals.
On auspicious festival days, such as the Puṣya full-moon festival,
accompanied by the great sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, along with songs.
One should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana) with auspicious emblems dedicated to Śiva;
as many parvan festivals as one performs this nīrājana for Śiva with devotion, [so many rewards shall one obtain].
He is glorified in the world of Rudra for as many thousands of years as there are [verses],
provided he performs singing and instrumental music at the three junctions of the day during the time of his ritual bath.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who performs dance, instrumental music,
or song— whether a hundred times or for as many days as he practices such dance and so forth.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [doses], one is glorified in the world of Rudra by means of the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass.
One should bathe [the Liṅga] with water purified by mantras; indeed, that is remembered as the Brahma-bath.
Whoever performs the Brahma-bath while worshipping the Liṅga for even a single day, [attains great merit].
Having quickly shaken off his sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
one should perform this repeatedly according to the prescribed rite with the five products of a tawny cow.

Bathing for the sake of the rites for the gods and the fire, as well as for eternal purification of the body, should be known to be a hundred times more meritorious than other forms of bathing; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should procure a tawny cow (kapilā), which is praised by sages, gods, and others.
Any Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapilā cow intended for the performance of rites dedicated to Śiva shall be cooked for a very long time in the most terrible ocean of hell.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years,
and whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of kalpas—
By performing a bath with ghee on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a man burns away all that [evil] just as fire consumes fuel; he who performs this ghee-bath upon the Liṅga even once.
Having rescued twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
one who practices yoga should give ten thousand milch cows to a master of the Vedas.
The fruit of bathing [the Linga] with milk for those who possess garments and gold is the same as that for a man who bathes the Linga once with a *āḍhaka* measure of milk.
By bathing the liṅga once with curd, one goes to the world of Soma in a silver celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed [the image] with honey, one is glorified in the world of the Moon.
One should bathe it with sesame oil produced by a hand-press.
One who performs the bathing of the Liṅga even once with white or yellow flour, or even with sugarcane juice, is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
The man who bathes the Liṅga even once with fruit-water shall attain the world of the Vidyādharas, endowed with all desires.
Having cast off the impurity of sin, one is honored in the world of the ancestors;
by bathing the Liṅga even once with white sacred ash, one rejoices.
Pure as the rays of the moon and glorious, he bathes the liṅga once with water filtered through a cloth, like Śiva in the lunar orb.
He whose soul is satisfied with all desires shall attain the world of Varuṇa,
he who bathes a liṅga even once with water infused with kuśa grass out of devotion.
One goes to the world of Brahmā by means of a golden celestial chariot;
one should bathe the Lord even once with water scented with sandalwood.
One attains the world of the Gandharvas and is honored by the Gandharvas;
[one attains] the realm of Savitṛ with water and flowers, and that of Kubera with golden water.
Having reached the world of Indra with water infused with jewels, he rejoices there;
[he enjoys] pāṭala, utpala, padma, and karavīra flowers at all times.
At the time of bathing, waters and the three types of milk should be employed;
having performed the bath with one of these three with devotion, O Śivā, three times.
Having shaken off the mire of evil, he is glorified in the world of Śiva—
he who bathes the Liṅga even once with water scented with camphor and agallochum.
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[he who worships] Śiva with pure water over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times.
Having bathed [the deity] once with devotion, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever bathes a Liṅga with cold water for the sake of the ancestors,
those ancestors, being satisfied, shall go from even hell to heaven.
Having bathed the *liṅga* with cold water, one should then bathe it with warm water;
after that, one should bathe it with ghee, for ghee itself is most excellent.
Having performed these three ablutions and having worshipped with devotion,
a person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A bath with copper vessels yields a hundred times more merit than one with earthen jars;
with silver, the merit is ten thousandfold greater; and with gold, the fruit is ten million times superior.
Beholding the Liṅga is meritorious; likewise, touching it after beholding it is so as well.
Worship through touch is superior, and bathing with ghee is even better than that;
by bathing with ghee, the sins committed by embodied beings in this world and the next are destroyed.
Since Śaṅkara destroys [sins], one should therefore perform a ritual bath;
he forgives ten offenses with water, but a hundred with milk.
One who performs the bath with curd forgives a thousand [offenses], and one with ghee forgives ten thousand;
however, he who performs the ghee-bath continuously for a month [forgives all].
Endowed with twenty-one lineages, one shall dwell happily in the city of Śiva.
It should be known that bathing yields a hundredfold fruit, while an oil massage yields twenty-fivefold.
At the conclusion of the fruits, a thousand-fold great bath is proclaimed;
one should perform a bath of ghee and an anointing with ghee, for the liṅga becomes free from deformity.
One should wash [the image] with powders derived from barley and wheat mixed with fragrant substances,
and one should also bathe it at intervals with pleasantly warm water.
One should rub [the image] with bilva leaves and likewise purify the pedestal;
one obtains the fruit that is gained by giving ten thousand cows.
One who offers to Śiva an oblation (arghya) accompanied by flowers and fruits obtains all the fruit resulting from the act of anointing the Liṅga.
One is glorified in the world of Śiva for ten thousand years.
[The offerings of] water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, ghee, curd, and rice grains [yield this result].
Sesame seeds and white mustard seeds likewise constitute the eightfold *arghya*;
when mixed with scented water, it becomes a hundred times superior to the ordinary water-offering (*udakārghya*).
The arghya water combined with the five products of the cow becomes a hundredfold more effective.
He who fills the eightfold arghya vessel and places it upon the head of the Liṅga [attains great merit].
One rejoices in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years by offering barley,
rice, paddy, beans, and unbroken grains.
Some authorities maintain that the offering should be accepted even without ghee if unbroken rice grains are present;
and whatever fruit may result from giving the arghya with a wooden vessel—
Therefore, the merit from offering with an earthen vessel is proclaimed to be tenfold;
by the gift of an arghya offering with a copper vessel, the merit is a hundred times greater.
An offering made with palāśa or lotus leaves is equal to one made with a copper vessel;
it should be understood that an offering made with a silver vessel is a hundred thousand times superior.
The arghya placed in a golden vessel possesses a merit a billion times greater;
likewise, the bathing water, arghya, food offerings, and the rites of bali and worship follow this same sequence.
And through the distinction of different vessels, that fruit becomes increasingly superior.
O Śivā,
for one who has mastered the Vedas, the gift of a silver vessel yields a hundred times the fruit of one who would give a hundred crores of gold.
The merit of one who gives silver to Śiva is even greater than that;
so too for one who, with devotion, offers golden vessels to Śiva.
It is not possible to measure that person's infinite merit in particular;
it is declared that the fruit for both the wealthy and the poor is equal when giving to Śiva.
Of those two as well, he who has greater devotion to Śiva is superior;
for even when wealth is available, he who, out of delusion, does not perform the ritual in detail [is inferior].
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit at all;
therefore, whatever has been performed with leaves, fruits, flowers, water, and so forth—
The fruit of that should be known as infinite; devotion alone is the cause here.
Having performed the smearing of the Liṅga with divine and fragrant scents, [one attains this result].
One is honored in the world of Raudra for a hundred divine crores of years;
however, the merit from anointing with sandalwood paste is twice that of other fragrant unguents.
It should be known that the merit from agallochum is eight times greater than that of sandalwood;
specifically, from black agallochum, a twofold fruit is desired.
Therefore, a hundredfold merit is ordained for saffron;
likewise for sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, when ground with saffron to a fine paste.
Having thoroughly smeared the *liṅga*, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million eons;
likewise, by fanning the *liṅga*—which has been anointed with fragrances—with a palm-leaf fan.
For ten thousand years he is honored in the world of Vāyu,
having offered a beautiful palm-leaf fan to Rudra with devotion.
By giving a peacock-feather fan that is exceedingly beautiful to Śiva, one is honored in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years; [by giving such a fan],
one is honored in the world of Rudra with the merit of a hundred billion years.
Having offered a fly-whisk to Śiva, adorned with a jeweled canopy and pavilions.
Listen to the fruit of his merit from [giving] a staff made of gold, silver, or other materials:
with the tips of his hands grasping chowries, he will be surrounded by celestial women.
Abiding in a celestial palace of great enjoyment, one shall dwell for a long time in the city of Śiva;
such is the accumulation of infinite merit through the practice of worship.
Sanatkumāra, tell me: with how many kinds of flowers should worship be performed?
Page 17 (20)
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
With flowers produced in the forest, or with leaves grown upon the mountains, [one should worship].
One should worship Śiva with flowers that have not been stale, are free from holes, have been sprinkled with water, are devoid of insects, and may even be those grown in one's own garden.
Merit becomes especially distinguished by the specific variety of flower offered to a worthy recipient who is endowed with austerity,
virtuous conduct, and good qualities, and who has mastered the Veda.
Whatever fruit is desired from giving ten pieces of gold in flowers,
that same fruit is obtained by offering even a single Arka flower to Śiva.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving ten pieces of gold,
a greater fruit than that shall be obtained through such a specific flower.
In this same way, the fruit to be known from other flowers should be understood; listen to that:
among a thousand *arka* flowers, the *karavīra* is superior;
among a thousand *bilva* leaves, a single *padma* is superior.
The *baka* flower is superior to thousands of lotus flowers.
Indeed, a single *dhuttūraka* flower is better than a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers;
a *bṛhatpuṣpa* is superior to a thousand *dhuttūraka* flowers.
The *droṇa* flower is superior to a thousand *bṛhat* flowers;
indeed, the *apāmārga* is superior to a thousand *droṇa* flowers.
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *apāmārga* flowers;
a single *śamī* flower is superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers.
Among thousands of *śamī* flowers, the glorious blue lotus is superior;
indeed, the blue lotus is the most excellent of all flowers.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses to Śiva.

For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas, that glorious one, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, shall dwell in the city of Śiva. Whatever fruit has been proclaimed for the remaining varieties of flowers, [he shall obtain that as well].
In accordance with the fruit thereof, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The Śamī flower and the blossom of the Bṛhatī are said to be equal; the Jātī, Vijayā, and Pāṭalā are to be known as equal to the Karavīra.
One should avoid white mandāra flowers, those produced from the karañja and indrataru trees, as well as vaibhītaka flowers and their leaves.
One should avoid flowers that are foul-smelling or have a pungent odor;
one should also avoid any fragrant flowers that are impure.
Even if it lacks fragrance, that which is pure, such as kuśa grass and the like, is sattvic; and that pure flower known as dhika is equal to it.
Gold and other such items are recommended to be offered at night to Śaṅkara;
all flowers except for the mallikā should be offered during the day, while the mallikā may be offered both by day and by night.
Day and night, they struck him with *karavīra* flowers that were infested with hair and insects, as well as those that were withered and stale.
One should discard flowers that have been plucked by oneself or those that are withered;
one should not worship the deity with buds, nor should one offer cooked food.
One should carefully discard any fruit that has been pierced by insects, even if it is ripe;
however, if flowers are not available, one may offer leaves as well.
If leaves are not available, one should offer fruits;
if even fruits are not available, one should offer grasses, shrubs, or medicinal herbs.
Even by the mere availability of herbs, he becomes worshipped through devotion;
for each individual flower offered, the fruit is ten gold pieces.
It is said that for those very same [offerings] when weighed on a scale, the fruit is twofold;
so too for one who thoroughly worships the Liṅga with fragrant flowers and loose blossoms.
Or even with very dense garlands, he shall obtain infinite fruit;
so too for one who worships the Liṅga even once with unbroken bilva leaves.
The man who worships the Linga even once with Dhattūra flowers is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having obtained the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cowries and attained auspiciousness, he shall go to Śiva—
he who worships the Liṅga even once with devotion using Bṛhatī flowers.
Having obtained the fruit of giving ten thousand cows, one shall go to Śiva;
[one should offer] jasmine, blue lotuses, red lotuses, jasmine, punnāga, and campaka flowers.
Aśoka, śveta-mandāra, karṇikāra, and bakula;
karavīra, arka, mandāra, śamī, tagara, and kesara.
Also the kuśa, apāmārga, kumuda, kadamba, and droṇaja;
as well as the saugandhika, āsana, nāga, bindu, śaivalikā, and arjuna.
The Tulasī, Kuravaka, Kola, Nāgavañjula, Nandyāvarta, Śamyāka, Tilaka, and Navamālikā;
A person should worship Śiva with whatever flowers are available, such as those of the *taru*, *puṇṇāga*, *dantī*, *mālatī*, *kuṭaja*, and others.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that he attains:
[he travels] in celestial chariots that resemble ten million suns and can go everywhere.
Encircled by garlands of flowers and resounding with the music of songs and instruments.

With the sweet sounds of lutes and musical instruments, filled with ten million Rudras who were languid from wandering at will— beings difficult even for gods and dānavas to attain— [the place was] crowded.
Being fanned with chowries and being praised by gods and asuras,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva, or wherever else may please him.
Or, having worshipped Śiva with devotion using these very flowers— both those growing in water and on land— that have been sprinkled [with consecrated water], one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should construct a very dense flower-pavilion over Śiva,
adorned with hanging flower garlands reaching down as far as the pedestal.
Moving above all, adorned with divine fragrances upon exceedingly lofty Mahāyāna vehicles, the glorious one does not remain in the city of Śiva as one who is merely happy.
O Śivā, he who, at the times of the sacred festivals, should fashion a covering for [the deity] with flowers arranged in many forms, radiant with various blossoms;
Surrounded by a retinue of a thousand Puṣpaka celestial chariots,
he was endowed with divine enjoyment of the three pleasures and possessed of delight in sport.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, his teaching unassailable;
in all worlds beginning with Śiva, he goes wherever he desires.
In all matters such as the arrangement of offerings, devotion, and ritual construction,
this fruit should be understood in brief according to one's wealth.
One should diligently worship the Liṅga and encircle the altar with garlands;
the altar becomes the Goddess, and the Liṅga is Maheśvara himself.
By worshipping those two, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped.
He who, having personally gathered flowers, worships Śiva himself, [attains the highest merit].
Śiva himself constantly accepts those offerings through devotion to him;
for that many thousands of years, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whoever should establish a grove for Śiva, adorned with mango, bilva, and other trees, as well as jasmine, vijayā, rājāka, karavīra, lotus, and arkakubjaka;
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of that [person] who [plants] punnāgas, nāgas, bakulas, aśokas, utpalas, campakas, plantains, hemapuṣpas, and so forth.
As many thousands of years as there are leaves, flowers, and fruits of the *nīpa* tree, for that long he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One should offer incense made from lac and substances derived from living beings repeatedly, O Śivā.
One obtains birth in the house of one who knows the four Vedas and remains constantly happy;
one should offer incense made of black agallochum and camphor once to Śivā.
Listen to the fruit of his merit for practicing this continuously for half a month:
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
At the end of that [life], that lord of the earth enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva;
indeed, Śaṅkara himself accepts the guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
By giving gifts for a month or half a month, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who burns guggulu resin with clarified butter on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—
Śiva [removes] even a thousand offenses committed here or in the hereafter.
Since Śaṅkara is forgiving, therefore one should always give to Śivā.
By offering devadāru, nameru, sarja, śrīvāsaka, kṛndrata,
and śrīphala mixed with clarified butter, one attains supreme prosperity.
To these [deities], one should offer fragrant incense of six thousand-fold superior quality;
agallochum (agaru) ten thousandfold, and black agallochum (asitāgaru) double that amount.
Guggulu should be ten thousand [units] with twice as much clarified butter;
one should regularly offer guggulu, especially when combined with ghee.
Having burned two thousand fruits of *guggulu* known as *mahiṣākṣa*, mixed with clarified butter, for one year, one becomes equal to Śiva.
By burning either a *nameru* tree mixed with clarified butter or a *bilva* tree,
a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One should undoubtedly purify a person joined with sin;
black agallochum burns away sin just as a fire of chaff burns away dross from gold.

One who should smear the entire city of Śiva within with excellent fragrances— including the door-panels, doors, walls, and so forth, both horizontally and vertically, along with the sacrificial altar (vedikā).
One should cause it to dwell with flower garlands and also with fragrant incenses;
listen now to the merit of whoever performs this even once.
With numerous Great Vehicles, perfectly fulfilling all desires and fragrant for a league [around], they filled all directions.
For a hundred divine millions of eons he is honored in the world of Śiva;
at its conclusion, by the remainder of his merit, he becomes the sovereign of the three worlds.
He who, at every change of season, constructs a temple of Śiva adorned with divine perfumes,
is honored in the world of Śiva together with his entire lineage.
Having given to Rudra a sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of triple-stranded white or beautiful yellow silk thread and the like, a man becomes one who has reached the end of the Vedas (*vedāntagā*).
O Śivā, one should offer garments that are most variegated, substantial, and soft— either two, three, or nine in number— and which are new and perfumed.
For as many thousands of years as there are threads in that garment, for so long one is honored in the world of Rudra.
He who would offer even a mere fragment of gold upon the head of the Liṅga shall occupy half the throne of Indra for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
In this very manner, the fruit should be understood in brief according to the sequence for all golden vessels and crowns in their entirety.
Whoever offers a cup made of arka leaves consecrated with the madhuparka mantra to Śarva shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One should prepare a prastha of śāli rice and cook it into well-prepared food;
one should offer that caru-oblation to Śiva, especially on the fourteenth lunar day.
One should offer turmeric-colored rice, kṛsara, white rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), and likewise *yācaka*, mixed with molasses, sugar-candy, and ghee; such items as these should be presented.
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
And when foods made with pieces of sugar-candy are offered, they are protected by ghee;
therefore, that [offering] is four times more meritorious than other foods.
For the purpose of food, fruits such as *mārjitā* and *pānaka* are desired;
half of that quantity is prescribed for the offering of scented water.
One should offer well-ripened fruits such as the mātuluṅga;
the fruit of that [offering] for Śiva is equal to the fruit obtained from offering edible foods.
By the gift of a ghee lamp to Śiva,
one crosses over the southern darkness extending for a hundred yojanas and attains a celestial chariot resplendent like the sun.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who offers betel leaf endowed with the five fragrances to Śiva and likewise to the Guru.
Possessing a fragrant luster, radiant, and beautiful in every limb,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years.
Whoever should prepare a beautiful garland of lamps with ghee during the month of Kārttika,
especially on the fourteenth day and the new moon day;
With a splendor resembling ten thousand suns, he illuminates the directions;
seated upon his celestial chariot as a mass of radiance, having uplifted his entire lineage,
he blazes forth once kindled with clarified butter equal in measure to the number of lamps.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are auspicious lamp-trees that one has erected in the temple of Śiva, for that long one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One obtains twice the merit compared to the former; there is no doubt about this—by lighting a lamp at that sacred site and offering a cluster of iron [flowers] in the temple of Śiva.
Having given [this] along with a silver vessel, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
one should carry a lamp upon the head before Śiva for the entire night.
With iron hands raised against his forehead and likewise against his chest,
he was adorned by celestial chariots as brilliant as ten thousand suns.
One is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred thousand divine aeons.
One should offer a beautifully crafted mirror before Śiva,
having adorned its perimeter with white garlands and sandalwood paste.
Stainless as the rays of the moon, glorious, fortunate, and assuming any form at will.
Having performed a circumambulation with devotion around the temple of Śiva, a man is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas.
O Śivā, a single prostration performed as a sacrifice is remembered as the best of all sacrifices; it easily yields the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
he who prostrates himself on the ground like a staff and offers his salutation with reverence.
The destination that one attains cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices;
it is the fruit found in all sacrifices, all fasts, and all the Vedas.
One shall obtain that fruit through praise, recitation, and offerings to Śiva;
one should offer a white horse after having decorated it with five colors.
Adorned with the tinkling sound of small bells and graced by a peacock-umbrella,
he stood above all the gods in a celestial chariot accompanied by a hundred others.
He who provides a canopy adorned with rows of banners in a temple of Śiva rejoices in heaven like Rudra for a thousand manvantaras.
Or else, one should offer eight great banners in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
together with a thousand celestial palaces, resplendent with divine banners,
one rejoices in heaven like Rudra for more than a hundred times ten thousand kalpas.
Pure as the rays of the autumnal moon and adorned with a network of pearls.
One should offer a parasol made of jewels or fashioned from gold and other precious materials,
held aloft by beautiful attendants under a variegated canopy.
If that embodied being, having long been happy in the city of Śiva with celestial chariots providing hundreds of enjoyments,
should thereafter desire sovereignty, he may do so upon the lapse of time.
He enjoys the earth bounded by the ocean under a single umbrella—
[the merit of one] who [offers] a great bell with a loud sound, joined with chains.
One should also fix an image made of bell-metal or iron in the abode of Śiva;
for the illustrious Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa is exceedingly dear to Śiva.
Having attained strength equal to Śiva, one shall dwell for a long time in the world of Śiva;
[one should offer] kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, timila-drums, and various musical instruments.
He who offers musical instruments made of bamboo, bell-metal, and other materials to Śiva,
shall [dwell] in celestial chariots with great enjoyments, accompanied by the sounds of flutes, lutes, and other instruments.
By the gift of women, songs, and especially musical instruments accompanied by sound, one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred times ten thousand yugas.
Having offered a pair of conchs along with a great-sounding drum at the abode of Śiva, one rejoices for an inexhaustible time in the world of Īśvara according to one's desire.
One is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for ten million aeons;
there is a celestial chariot, radiant like a white lotus, adorned in the center with water-jars.
It may be of various colors or of a single color, adorned with new garments and the like,
and decorated with hanging cords, strings, bells, and chowries.
Whoever should offer [a gift] upon Śiva, or even arrange it before him,
shall rejoice like Rudra in all the worlds for ten million eons.
Whoever should offer above Śiva [an umbrella] adorned with all kinds of jewels,
equipped with the sound of tinkling bells, and embellished with moon-shaped ornaments;

Listen to the meritorious fruit of one who constructs a beautiful pavilion adorned with pearls: he shall dwell within millions upon millions of celestial palaces, enriched by the fulfillment of all desires.
One shall dwell in the city of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings;
one should establish a shrine for Śarva, adorned with offerings of flowers and garments.
With garments such as dukūla, paṭṭa, or devāṅga, or with cloths endowed with colors;
indeed, for as many threads as there are in the cloth, the silk, and so forth—
For as many thousands of yugas as there are, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having praised Śiva, the entire universe is sustained by means of rain.
With what intention the world performs the fire-rite,
that same merit shall accrue to one who constructs a most beautiful brick temple for the fire of Rudra.
By performing the fire-ritual there even once, one shall attain union with Śiva;
he who performs the fire-ritual for Śiva secures his own longevity.
One is liberated from extensive sins by means of the white, auspicious ashes,
having fashioned ten mandalas at the edge of a temple of Śiva.
One should constantly offer them a bali-oblation accompanied by all ritual offerings;
one should prepare a copper vessel provided with flowers, incense, and water.
And on all sides [he placed] Rudra, the hosts of Mothers, and the guardians of the quarters.
Whoever performs this offering of bali even once in the ten directions is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand years.
Having performed the fierce twilight offering (saṃdhyā-bali) daily or on festival days at night,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand aeons. A liṅga made of curd-rice, placed in golden vessels and the like, [is likewise honored].
Having honored it with flowers and incense, and adorned it above with a canopy.
Carrying the bowl upon his head, he proceeded slowly in a clockwise direction as far as the temple of Śiva, amidst the sounds of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Adorned with mirrors, banners, garlands, and the like, beautified by songs, dances, and so forth, as well as with umbrellas, chowries, incense, and likewise with staffs, lamps, and other such items.
Standing before the *liṅga*, one should offer a *bali* in all directions with the remaining curd-rice mixed with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
By this fierce offering, the Mothers, the Rudras, Śiva, Umā, Ṣaṇmukha, and the others, being well-pleased, always partake in peace.
Removing a garland from Śiva and wiping [the image] at the conclusion of worship—
each one of these acts is equal to the fruit of a Cāndrāyaṇa fast.
Having prepared a small Śiva-maṇḍala measuring one cubit in front of Śiva,
he should scatter it with unbroken rice grains, flowers, or even leaves alone.
By performing this once, a man shall obtain birth in the house of one who knows the four Vedas, becoming handsome, fortunate, illustrious, radiant, a knower of the Vedas, and happy.
Having thus adorned the ground in the temple of Śiva with svastikas, lotuses, and the like,
made from colored powders and flour, the merit shall be a hundredfold greater than before.
Having given even a small or a large amount of equipment for the sacrifice to Śiva,
one is thus honored in the world of Śiva according to one's wealth.
What wonder is there that whatever is given with Śiva in view— the cause of all causes— yields infinite fruit for the donor?
Whatever is desired, whatever is excellent, and whatever has been acquired through righteous means—
that should be offered to Śiva with devotion by those who seek no other fruit.
Even one who acts with deceitful intent toward Śiva’s abode, whether by labor or by payment of wages,
goes to heaven free from sin through that very deed, provided he is free from deceit.

Beings that were utilized in the work of constructing temples for Śiva— such as those employed in digging wells, planting groves, and providing food and drink— as well as those involved in digging and uprooting [trees] and so forth;
Even without desire, all things, both stationary and moving,
go to heaven by the grace of the Supreme Lord; of this there is no doubt.
The sacred field of Śiva extends for more than fifty *liṅgas* in every direction; for embodied beings, death there is the cause of attaining union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).
This measurement of the sacred field (kṣetra) is prescribed for a liṅga installed by human beings;
it shall be one thousand [yojanas] for a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, and half of that for one established by a seer (ārṣa).
Even one of evil conduct who dwells in that hermitage of Śiva goes to the supreme abode; therefore, it is known as Śivapura.
Therefore, one should certainly construct a dwelling near a sacred field of Śiva;
for the water situated near a Śiva-liṅga is auspicious when it flows forward.
That should be known as Śivagaṅgā; having bathed therein, one shall go to Śiva. Furthermore, whoever constructs a large pond or even a well at a Śiva-hermitage [attains the same].
Having abandoned everything other than Śiva, with a mind solely intent on Śiva, one is glorified in the world of Śiva together with seven times three generations of one's kin.
One who desires his own welfare should perform the ritual of worship of Śiva;
for life passes swiftly, and youth passes swiftly.

Disease approaches swiftly; therefore, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped. As long as death has not arrived, as long as old age has not overcome you, and as long as there is no impairment of the senses—worship Śaṅkara during that time.
There is no other dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in the three worlds;
having understood this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort.
Those who are devoted to Śiva—the Lord of the God of Gods, the peaceful, unborn, and sovereign Master—[attain the highest state].
Always worshipping with devotion, their minds fixed on that and established in austerity,
they attain happiness in this world and go to the supreme goal.
Having worshipped the Lord of Creatures with a joyful inner soul,
one should, with palms joined in reverence, recite this hymn of praise.
I bow to Sadāśiva— the auspicious one, the maker of auspiciousness, the peaceful, whose very self is auspicious, the supreme auspiciousness,
and the guide upon the path to auspiciousness.
I bow down to Śaṅkara— the eternal, the beautiful, the pure, the teacher, the dryer of faults, the universe itself, the Lord of the lords of the universe.
I perpetually bow to the Lord, the supreme remover of all sins, the excellent dispeller of all diseases,
the eternal remover of all suffering, and the best of those who relieve the distressed.

I bow to Sthāṇvīśa, who is established in the distinction between the non-abiding and the abiding, who is the manifestation of stability and duration, and who dwells in the yoga that abides in mere steadfastness.
I bow down to Īśāna, the supreme deity, the lord, the leader of mantras, the sovereign of all beings, the Īśāna.
The support for the attainment of all goals, the leader of the hosts, the bestower of boons,
the son of Rudra, the god, the guide, and the Vināyaka.
May he always perform for me pacification, security, and the accomplishment of all activities—
[the deity] who resembles a sapphire, has three eyes, and brandishes a blazing trident as his weapon.
Clad in red garments, glorious, with a dark-complexioned body and adorned with serpent ornaments,
he stood like Viṣṇu himself, with a rosary resting upon his head.
May Mahākāla, with a gracious mind, grant me peace— He who is incomparable in dispelling evil and in destroying the stain of misfortune.
Having the luster of the color of a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon, with a neck possessing the brilliance of an emerald;
four-faced, four-armed, three-eyed, and radiant on all sides— may he, being pleased, grant me great peace with a gracious mind.
The Lord of the Earth is the god Vṛṣa, the highest among all supreme dharmas;
because he bears the Lord upon his back, Dharma is therefore the lord of the world.
May the illustrious Bull,
the bearer of the bull, the omniscient one, who is equal to all, the omnipresent, the lord born of Śarva, grant me peace.
The pacifier of enemy armies, the teacher, may he grant me peace;
being pleased with a joyful mind, may he grant me great peace.
Clad in yellow garments, in the form of a maiden, and well-adorned;
the Mother of the Gaṇas, Ambikā, the three-eyed one, the peaceful Gaurī, the sovereign of the gods.
May the Goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments, supreme in her grace and most excellent, grant me peace; may my Mother swiftly bestow success.
With a glossy dark-blue complexion, she is the crusher of the great buffalo;
she wields a bow and a discus as weapons, and carries a sword and a shield.
May she who holds a threatening hand raised, the destroyer of all calamities,
the mother of all auspiciousness, swiftly bestow welfare upon me.
With a fleshless body, his sinews and bones firmly bound together,
he was exceedingly subtle, possessed of great speed, and the best of Kirīṭins, who agitated the three eyes [of Śiva].
Possessing the nature of Rudra, the vigor of Rudra, and a mind solely intent upon Rudra,
may he certainly bring about auspiciousness through his state of being the inner controller of these [elements].
The great Caṇḍeśvara is the lord of the fierce Gaṇa army,
the bearer of a large skull and an eye, with a rosary placed in his hand and possessing three eyes.
May the Great Yogi, who removes even the most fierce sins and purifies such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, grant me a succession of auspicious blessings.
Seated upon a lotus, resembling gold, with four lotus-like faces,
holding a water-pot, glorious, and worshipped by gods and gandharvas.
May Brahmā, who is ever devoted solely to the meditation on Śiva and intent upon the worship of Śiva,
grant me peace through his divine word, "Brahman."
Seated upon Tārkṣya, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
dark-complexioned, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with a forest garland.
The god Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, is the supreme deity of sacrifice.
Having the appearance of black collyrium, he bore the marks of a sword belonging to Śiva;
endowed with the grace of Śiva, he was solely devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
May Viṣṇu, who is eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva, grant me peace;
may the Goddess, whose luster is like a ruby and whose face is a four-petalled lotus, do the same.
With her hands offering a rosary and holding a water-pot,
the auspicious Brahmāṇī has a gentle countenance and is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
May she, being pleased, grant me peace at all times through the sound of the Veda—
she who resembles the snowy mountain, the goddess whose face is a four-petalled lotus, her hands holding a rosary and an auspicious water-pot.
Tall, with a gentle countenance, and devoted to the worship of Śiva,
may she, being pleased, always grant me peace through the sound of the Veda.
The Goddess, who resembles the snowy mountain and is borne by a great bull—
Holding a trident in her hand, she grants boons and is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
The Great Goddess is a devotee of Rudra, always intent upon the worship of Rudra;
she has four arms, four faces, and three eyes, and she is the remover of sins.
May the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, pleased with me, remove my distress—
she who is the goddess borne upon a peacock, her form as red as vermilion.
Holding a spear in her hand, possessed of great heroism, and adorned with all ornaments,
she is a devotee of Rudra, highly meritorious, and always intent upon the worship of Rudra.
May the goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, swiftly grant me peace;
she holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, is dark-complexioned, wears yellow garments, and is auspicious.
Four-armed, seated upon Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī is worshipped by the gods;
she is eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva, her mind fixed solely on Rudra.
May she who crushes all asuras, who has the snout of a boar, who is formidable, and who rides upon an excellent boar, grant me constant peace.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with expansive form, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
she constantly threatens all obstacles while perpetually worshipping Sadāśiva.
May the goddess Vārāhī, the bestower of boons, grant me security and health;
she is mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, holds a thunderbolt in her hand, and possesses great strength.
Adorned with a thousand eyes, possessing a golden luster,
saluted by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and graced with excellent ornaments.
May the goddess Aindrī always swiftly bestow peace upon me.
Śyāma, wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland,
is the supreme deity among the gods of sacrifice— Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu.
Having the appearance of black collyrium, he was characterized by the play of Śiva and Śivā;
endowed with the grace of Śiva, he was solely devoted to the meditation on Śiva.

May Viṣṇu, who is eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva, grant me peace. May the auspicious Goddess, possessing the luster of a ruby, with four lotus-like faces, her hands holding a rosary and bearing a water-pot, bestow blessings.
May Brahmāṇī, who possesses a gentle countenance and is devoted to the worship of Śiva,
being pleased, always grant me peace through the sound of the word "Brahman."
The goddess, resembling a snow-clad mountain, possesses four lotus-like faces;
her auspicious hands are joined with a rosary and she holds a water-pot.

Possessing a gentle countenance and devoted to the worship of Śiva, may she, being pleased by the sound of the word "Brahman," grant me peace at all times. The Goddess, who resembles a snow-clad mountain and is borne upon a great bull—
Holding a trident in her hand and granting boons, she is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
The Great Goddess is a devotee of Rudra, always intent upon the worship of Rudra;
she has four arms, four faces, and three eyes, and she is the remover of sins.
May the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who removes my afflictions, be pleased with me—
she who rides upon a peacock and whose form is as red as vermilion.
Holding a spear in her hand, possessed of great heroism, adorned with all ornaments,
devoted to Rudra, highly meritorious, and ever intent on the worship of Rudra—
may the goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, swiftly grant me peace.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments,
auspicious, four-armed, mounted upon Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī is worshipped by the gods.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, with her mind solely fixed on Rudra,
may she who crushes all Asuras grant me perpetual peace.
She has the snout of a boar, she is formidable, and she rides upon an excellent boar;
she is dark and radiant, vast in form, and holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Constantly threatening obstacles and always worshipping Śiva,
may the boon-granting goddess Vārāhī bestow upon me security and health;
she who is mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, holds a thunderbolt in her hand, and possesses great strength.
Adorned with a thousand eyes, possessing a golden luster,
bowed to by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and graced with excellent ornaments—
may the goddess Aindrī always grant me peace.
With hair standing on end and fierce eyes, fleshless and bound together by sinews,
with a gaping and terrible face, she wields a sword and a shield.
The goddess Kapālamālinī is fierce, bearing a khaṭvāṅga staff;
her eyes are reddish-brown, and she is draped in an elephant hide.
Her limbs are adorned with various serpent-sacrificial threads; she dwells in the abode of the departed spirits;
in her terrible form as a jackal, she strikes fear with her jackal-like howls.
May Cāmuṇḍī, in her fierce form, provide great protection for me;
likewise may the Ākāśamātṛ goddesses, who are the sole mothers of the world, protect me.
All the Mothers of beings, as well as the other divine Mothers—
the entire host of goddesses who are the mothers of all— stand with weapons in their unhesitating hands.
Desirous of offerings and possessing great prosperity, they abide pervading the world; they are devotees of Rudra, [worshippers] of the Great Goddesses, and solely intent on the worship of Rudra.
May the Mothers, worshipped by the gods, grant me constant peace—
those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in terrible places.
Those who are gentle and those who dwell in gentle places,
the Mothers of fierce form, the lords of the Gaṇas,
and likewise others who have become obstacles and reside in the ten directions— [all these were summoned].
May all of you, with delighted minds, accept my offering;
may you grant me success eternally and always protect me from fears.
In the eastern direction, there is a host of those with thunderbolts in hand, possessed of great strength;
they have very white eyes, appear white in complexion, and are likewise white and red.
May those who dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld,
being devoted to the worship of Rudra, always grant me security and peace.
All those hosts in the south-eastern quarter have sacrificial ladles in their hands and carry quivers; they have very red eyes, resemble blood-red in hue, and are indeed crimson and dark red.
May those who dwell in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of Pātāla—
who are ever intent on bowing to Rudra— grant me peace at all times.
And may those hosts in the southern direction, who constantly hold the staff in their hands, [grant me peace].
Those with very black eyes, those resembling black, and likewise those who are blackish-red;
those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.
May those whose minds are worshipped by Rudra always bring me auspiciousness; and may those hosts of Rākṣasas in the southwest, who carry swords in their hands, do the same.
Some resemble dark-blue lac or sapphire, while others are blue and red;
they dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, on the earth, and in the depths of the netherworld.
May those who are devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord always grant me protection;
and may those hosts in the western direction, who constantly hold nooses in their hands, do the same.
Those with beautiful dark eyes, those resembling the color of darkness, as well as those who are reddish-brown—
those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, on earth, and in the depths of the netherworld.
May all those devoted to Śiva grant me constant well-being;
and may those Gaṇas in the northwestern quarter, who always hold banners in their hands, do the same.
Some had very smoky eyes, some resembled smoke, and others were smoke-colored and red;
they dwelt in the heavens, the atmosphere, on the earth, and in the depths of the netherworld.
May the great-souled devotees of Śiva perform a rite of pacification for me;
and may those Gaṇas in the north, who are the constant guardians of treasures, do the same.
With eyes that are beautifully yellow, they are indeed yellowish in appearance and likewise reddish-yellow;
they dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, on the earth, and in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla).
May all those who delight in devotion to Śiva always grant me well-being;
and may those hosts in the northeast, who constantly hold tridents in their hands, likewise do so.
Those with extremely subtle eyes, those resembling subtle forms, and likewise those who are subtly red;
those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld (pātāla).
May the gods of the northeast, to whom I bow, grant me constant peace;
and may those hosts below, who always hold discs in their hands, likewise do so.
With eyes that were deep yellow, they appeared yellowish, and likewise reddish-yellow;
they were celestial, atmospheric, terrestrial, and dwellers of the depths of Pātāla.
Those devoted to Śiva should perform the destruction of the stain of misfortune (alakṣmī);
for those who are the Gaṇas in the upper portion always hold lotuses in their hands.
Those with beautiful lotus-eyes, those resembling lotuses, and those as red as lotuses—
those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworlds.
May these noble-souled Gaṇas, endowed with great strength and prowess, who are intent upon the worship of Śiva, destroy my inauspiciousness.
Having worshipped Śiva with diligence, one should offer them a bali-oblation;
then those great-souled ones, being pleased, [bestow] peace, longevity, strength, and prosperity.
