It bestows [boons] quickly upon mortals, especially upon those who are devoted;
the city Amarāvatī is situated in the eastern quarter.
It was crowded with hosts of Vidyādharas, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
constructed with jeweled walls, and adorned with great gems.
There, the glorious lord of the gods, possessing a thunderbolt in his hand and endowed with great strength,
shone with a beautiful thousand eyes.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, golden-hued and of great splendor,
the Lord of Devas is ever joyful and devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord.
Devoted solely to the meditation on Śiva and dedicated to devotion to Śiva,
he was accompanied by other devotees of Śiva as well as by the gods and their followers.
May he who is devoted to bowing to Śiva perform my rite of pacification;
in the southeastern quarter lies the auspicious city of Tejovatī.
Crowded with multitudes of various colors and blazing with the radiance of jewels,
there stands the god Jvalana (Fire), who bestows prosperity upon embodied beings and destroys sin; his body is enveloped in flames, and his splendor is like that of glowing coals.
May the Lord, who is intent upon the worship of Śiva and permeated by the remembrance of Śiva,
grant me peace as well as the complete destruction of my sins.
To the south stands the city named Vaivasvatī,
the abode of the hosts of gods and asuras, and of the ancestors, rakshasas, and serpents.
Therein [is he] resembling a sapphire, with long eyes red at the corners,
mounted upon a great buffalo, and adorned with black garlands, garments, and ornaments.
May the illustrious Yama, of great splendor and devoted solely to the worship of Śiva,
being fully intent on the worship of Śiva, grant me well-being and health.
In the southwestern direction, however, lies the auspicious city of Kṛṣṇavatī,
crowded with hosts of great rākṣasas and teeming with piśācas and pretas.
There, he resembled a cloud, adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments.
With sword in hand, possessed of great splendor, and radiant with a formidable countenance,
the lord of the Rakshasas, Nirṛti, is eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva.
May he, intent upon devotion to Śiva, grant me great peace.
In the western quarter lies the auspicious city of Śuddhavatī,
crowded with various hosts of nāgas and frequented by various kinnaras.
There, he resembled a pearl and had deep reddish-brown eyes.
Clad in white garments, holding a noose in his hand, and possessed of great strength, may Varuṇa— with his mind solely fixed on Śiva through supreme devotion—
always destroy my afflictions of disease, grief, and distress.
In the division of the northwest direction lies the auspicious city Gandhavatī,
resounding with golden ramparts and frequented by hosts of Ṛṣis and Siddhas.
There, with a copper-colored body and dark-brown eyes,
his inner self pervaded by the Supreme and dependent upon it, he stood ready for battle with a banner-staff raised as a weapon.
May Pavana, the supreme deity, who is meditated upon as the Supreme Lord,
grant me security, health, strength, peace, and likewise victory.
To the north lies the city named Mahodayā, exceedingly radiant,
crowded with many yakṣas, and adorned with various jewels.
There the god stood, mace in hand, adorned with variegated garlands, garments, and ornaments;
he was short-armed, possessed of great splendor, and had deep reddish-brown eyes.
May the glorious Kubera, the granter of boons who is devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet,
being pleased and tranquil, grant me peace through his peaceful splendor.
There is a city named Yaśovatī situated in the northeastern direction;
it is filled with various hosts of attendants and contains dwellings fashioned from diverse jewels.
Extending as far as the wall of radiance, it was endowed with incomparable qualities;
there [sat] one resembling a pearl, with the moon made into his crest-ornament.
The three-eyed Hara, whose nature is peaceful, who bears a rosary,
is Īśāna, the supreme deity, the highest among all the best of gods.
May he also, through his all-pervading nature, swiftly grant me peace for those who dwell in the Bhūrloka,
the Bhuvarloka, and the Svargaloka.
May those who dwell in Maharloka, Janarloka, and Tapoloka, endowed with the power to bestow divinity upon the gods and others, always grant me peace.
May those joyful gods also always grant me peace,
as well as the gods in the realm of truth (Satyaloka) whose bodies are radiant with sublime splendor.
May the devotees of Śiva, who are well-disposed and radiant, grant me peace forever;
and those gods in the world of Tapas who illuminate the ten directions.
May those gods in Janaloka, who possess the luster of purified gold and whose minds are fixed solely on Śiva, pacify this great fear.
May those gods who eternally bow to the Lord and reside in their radiant celestial chariots in Maharloka always grant me peace.
May those gods of the heavenly realm, who are radiant and possessed of great power, and who are devoted to bowing before Bhava, destroy my fear.
May those gods who constantly bow to Śaṅkara and who shine throughout the ten directions in the Bhuvarloka grant me victory.
May those who dwell in the mountain caves and difficult terrains within the world of mortals, their minds fixed solely on Śiva, pacify this great fear.
May the gods, who are devoted to the worship of Rudra, always grant me protection.
May Sarasvatī, who is devoted to Śiva and possesses a pure mind and a body as white as the rays of the autumn moon, grant me all my desires.
May the Goddess Śrī— the splendor of those whose minds are intent on devotion to Śiva, possessing the luster of beautiful gold and hands like lotus-buds— grant me prosperity.
May the Goddess, who is devoted to Śiva, who is associated with Varuṇa, whose face is like the moon, and who is radiant with variegated gold, always grant all my desires.
With a most variegated necklace and a radiant golden girdle.
May Aparājitā, who is devoted to Rudra, grant me victory;
she is the color of vermilion-red, with long, blood-red eyes.
The glorious thousand-rayed one, whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses, the Lord garlanded with beams of light,
is devoted to worship through devotion to Śiva.
May she grant me great peace and ward off the afflictions of the planets;
for she is the nourisher of the world, cool as the vessel of nectar.
May Soma, with his gentle disposition, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
may the Lord with tawny eyes do so with his ruby-colored body.
Aṅgāraka was constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra;
he was endowed with the true nature of Rudra, and his mind was solely intent on the meditation of Rudra.
May he, glorious with a body as radiant as saffron and perfectly proportioned, forever destroy all fear and affliction caused by the planets for me.
May the wise Bṛhaspati, a devotee of Śiva, likewise dispel the affliction caused by the planets—
he who possesses the luster of molten gold, whose abode is all-encompassing knowledge,
and who is ever intent upon the worship of Īśāna.
He too, with a peaceful mind, was supremely composed in meditation.
Having completely overcome the affliction of the planets, may he grant me victory! Shukra,

who possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and who is worshipped by the lords of both gods and demons— may he, through his constant worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction of the planets.
His complexion was like that of crushed collyrium, and the luster of his eyes was blood-red.
May Śanaiścara, a devotee of Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
may the exceedingly powerful Saiṃhikeya, who resembles a dark blue cloud, [grant protection].
May Rāhu, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
he resembles crushed collyrium, is glorious, holds a meteor in his hand, and possesses great strength.
May Ketu— who is ablaze, filled with smoky flames, yet ever devoted to the worship of Śiva—
dispel the affliction of the planets with his perfectly tranquil mind.
Smoky-colored, eternally fierce, the son of Death and possessed of great strength—
may Ketu, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction of the planets.
May these great-souled planets, who are devoted to the worship of Śiva and who always desire my welfare, grant me peace with joyful hearts.
Kṛttikā is the supreme goddess; Rohiṇī has a beautiful countenance;
the auspicious Mṛgaśiras is glorious; and Ārdrā is most radiant.
Punarvasu, as well as Puṣyā and the exceedingly powerful Āśleṣā—
these are the Mothers of the Constellations (Nakṣatramātaraḥ), who exist adorned with garlands of radiance.
Devoted to the worship of Mahādeva and empowered by the majesty of Mahādeva,
may these goddesses, stationed in the eastern quarter, always grant me peace.
Makhā is endowed with all virtues; Pūrvaphalgunī is incomparable;
Uttarāphalgunī is most excellent; and likewise, Hasta and Citrā are supreme.
Svāti, Viśākhā, and Varadā, situated on the right,
always worship the supreme three-eyed God.
May these constellations, impelled by Śiva, perform pacification for me as well—
Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlā, endowed with the power of supernatural success.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā possesses great power, and Uttarāṣāḍhā is auspicious;
the lunar mansion named Abhijit is most excellent, and Śravaṇa is supremely radiant.
These goddesses, radiant and beautiful in form, shine from the western direction;
well-cultivated, they worship Īśāna at all times. May they, being composed, bestow peace and prosperity.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvābhādrapadā,
as well as Uttarābhādrapadā, Revatī, and Aśvinī are of great power.
And the highly powerful Bharaṇī is always situated to the north;
they are constantly engaged in the worship of Śiva and are solely intent on meditation upon Śiva.
May those who bring about the arising of auspiciousness grant me peace at all times, forever:
Aries, the Lord of Beasts (the Lion), and the Archer, the best among the radiant ones.
These auspicious ones, devoted to the yoga of Śiva, illuminate the eastern quarter;
may they always perform what is beneficial for those intent on the worship of Hara’s feet.
The Maiden, the Bull, the God, and the Makara, all possessed of great supernatural power— may these, who always worship Śiva on the southern side with supreme devotion, grant me eternal peace.
Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius are situated in the west;
may they, who are devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet, always grant me well-being.
Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces—these are situated in the north.
They always worship Rudra, the leader of the world;
may those who impart the knowledge of Rudra grant me constant peace.
May the seven renowned sages, culminating in Dhruva, who are supremely radiant and endowed with the grace of Śiva, grant me peace at all times.
Kaśyapa, Gālava, Gārgya, Viśvāmitra the great sage,
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Mataṅga, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Nārada, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, Bharadvāja, the sage Aṅgiras, Vālmīki, Kauśika, Kaṇva, Śākalya, and then Punarvasu; p. 35(38).
Dūrvāsas, Śṛṅgaśṛṅga, Tṛṇabindu, Vimaṇḍaka, Daṇḍin, Pippalāda, Yājñavalkya, and Gautama.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Jāmadagnya, Pulastya, Saumari, Śubha, Agastya, Jaimini, Vyāsa, Marīci, Jahnu,
and Śālaṅkāyana— these and other such sages were ascetics devoted to penance.
May the highly fortunate wives of the sages, the daughters of the sages, and the young sons of the sages— who are devoted to meditation upon and worship of Śiva— always grant me peace.
May the hosts of Siddhas, those of perfected asceticism, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases, who are constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, always grant me peace.
The high-souled Vidyādharas and Garuḍa of great supernatural power—
all these are devoted to Maheśvara and worship Maheśvara as their supreme goal.
May they, who are devoted to bestowing blessings, swiftly grant success!
[There are] Namuci, the king of the Daityas, and the mighty Śaṅkukarṇa.
There was a famous Daitya named Mahānāda, possessed of supreme valor,
who was constantly devoted to the worship of the god Hāṭakeśvara.
May those of great supernatural power quickly bestow strength and vigor upon me:
Mahājambha, Hyagrīva, Prahlāda the lord and king of the Daityas,
Tāraka, the Daitya Agnimukha, Kālanemi, and likewise Bali.
May these high-souled Daityas, the enemies of the gods, who are permeated by the true nature of Śiva,
bestow upon us nourishment, strength, and valor.
Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Suparvan, and Pulomaka;
Mucukunda, Sukunda, and likewise the Daitya Raivataka.
With the highest devotion, they worship the supreme Śiva;
may those of pure nature always grant me constant nourishment.
May the illustrious wives of the Daityas, the auspicious daughters of the Daityas,
and those who are the sons of the Daityas, also grant me peace.
The king of serpent-lords, Ananta, whose eyes have red corners, is not colored by blood on his body; he is devoted to the worship and adoration of Śiva.
Having destroyed the poison of great sins, may he swiftly grant me peace;
with a perfectly white body, a crest-jewel of brilliant white gems,
displaying the majestic pride of beautiful serpents, and adorned with the lovely ornaments of Hara.
May Vāsuki, the lord of the Nāgas and a great devotee supreme in the worship of Śiva,
destroy all the poison of the Nāgas and grant me security and health.
With a body of deep yellow hue, shimmering with abundant enjoyments and wealth,
and with a brilliance exceedingly radiant, he was marked with the sign of a dancing svastika.
May the glorious Takṣaka, king of the nāgas, surrounded by ten million nāgas,
bring about for me great peace that removes all defects and poisons.
With an exceedingly black body and a throbbing, formidable head,
he possessed three lines upon his neck and stood with terrible fangs raised, ready for combat.
May the great nāga Kārkoṭaka, endowed with the power of poison and pride,
destroy the torment of poison, weapons, and fire, and grant me peace.
With a body the color of a lotus and beautiful, lotus-like eyes,
he possessed the auspicious mark of a lotus-pattern on his neck, appearing like a drop of nectar.
The renowned great nāga Padma, who delights in worshipping the feet of Hara,
may he grant me great peace and the destruction of the poison of great sins.
With bodies resembling white lotuses and possessing immeasurable splendor,
they are always adorned on their heads with the beautiful conch, trident, and lotus.
May Mahāpadma, the great Nāga, who is eternally devoted to Paśupati,
swiftly grant me peace after having utterly conquered his terrible poison.
Dark-complexioned in body, yet glorious with his necklace, he has lotus-like eyes;
intoxicated by the pride and strength of his poison, he bears a single line upon his neck.
Illuminated by the splendor of Śaṅkhapāla and others, the worshiper of the lotus feet of Śiva,
having destroyed the most terrible great poison, may he grant me peace.
With a body of exceeding whiteness, his head fashioned from the crescent moon,
adorned with the coils of a blazing serpent, and marked with auspicious characteristics.
May Gulika, the lord of the Naga kings, who is eternally devoted to Hara,
remove this terrible poison and grant me peace.
And those nāgas who are in the atmosphere, those nāgas who dwell in heaven, those nāgas who reside in mountain caves and difficult terrains, those nāgas who abide in the sky,
and those nāgas who dwell in the netherworld— all of them are concentrated here.
May those who are engaged in the worship of the feet of Hara always grant me peace.
May the female nāgas, the nāga maidens, and likewise the young nāgas—
devoted to Śiva and well-disposed— always grant me peace.
Whoever should proclaim or even hear this description of the Naga-formation,
that person Nagas will never harm, and poison will never overcome them.
One constantly obtains whatever is thought of, and likewise there shall be the destruction of evil;
they also bestow accomplishment free from all obstacles.
The goddess Surabhī, endowed with auspicious marks, dwells in Goloka;
she is constantly rich with streams of milk and is worshipped by the hosts of Brahman-sages.
Constantly surrounded by joyful herds of cows and bulls,
ever peaceful and devoted to Śiva, may she swiftly grant me peace.
May all these herds of cows and the bulls of great power—
high-souled devotees of Śiva— grant me constant peace.
O Goddess, you bestow the merit of the Gaṅgā; you are the rivers Yamunā and Narmadā, as well as the Gomatī, Tāpī, Peṇṇā, Varuṇā, and the excellent Devikā.
The great rivers, permeated by the true nature of Śiva, worship the Lord who is the master of all beings, the Supreme Lord, Maheśvara.
May they grant me constant peace as well as the complete destruction of my sins;
may they swiftly bestow upon me accomplishment, free from all obstacles.
The Candrabhāgā is of great merit, as is the auspicious river Godāvarī;
the Sarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Kauśikī, and Sarasvatī are most excellent.
May these highly blessed rivers, devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet and with their minds solely intent on meditation upon Śiva, grant me constant peace.
The river named Nairañjanā, the great river Śoṇa, and the supreme Mandākinī— all these auspicious waters are situated nearby.
May these and other rivers— those belonging to the earth, the heavens, and the intermediate space— who are constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra, perform my propitiation.
May those secret sacred sites, as well as the oceans and lakes,
all presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, perform rites of pacification.
The yakṣa Mahāvaiśravaṇa, the king of yakṣas, possessed of great supernatural power,
surrounded by a retinue of ten million yakṣas and joined by an incalculable number of yakṣas.
Endowed with great wealth, he was devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet;
he was solely intent on meditation upon Hara, and his supreme excellence lay in bowing at Hara’s feet.
May the great yakṣa Māṇibhadra, adorned with jewels and gems, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, being pleased, grant me peace.
He shone with a captivating necklace resting upon his neck;
he was constantly devoted to the singing of Śiva's praises and a perpetual worshiper of Śiva’s lotus feet.
May he who wards off all defects, his form surrounded by yakṣiṇīs and yakṣa maidens, grant me constant peace.
May the devotee who is intent on the worship of Rudra perform my rite of pacification;
may the great yakṣa Suvīra, adorned with jeweled earrings, do so as well.
On his forehead, he shone with a golden fillet of refined gold;
surrounded by many yakṣas, his form was bowed down to by yakṣas.
May the lord of yakṣas named Cāṇḍika, whose ear-rings shine with bracelets and who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, perform my pacification.
Adorned with a variegated crown and two armlets,
he was accompanied by yakṣa maidens and joined by an innumerable host of yakṣas.
May the illustrious Yakṣa Vibhaṇḍaka, adorned with various jewels and devoted to the worship of Hara, perform the rite of pacification for me.
His two ears shine eternally with a pair of beautiful earrings;
he is the lord of the Yakṣas, the master of the Yakṣas, the powerful commander of the Yakṣa army.
May the illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great Yakṣa, the lord and master of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, who is devoted to the feet [of the Buddha], perform peace for me.
Clad in divine silken garments and adorned with jewels and gold,
he was a devotee of Śiva, meditating upon Śiva and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Endowed with the grace of Śiva, may he perform my rite of pacification.
The great yakṣa Pūrṇabhadra is adorned with all ornaments.
His body was resplendent with a golden turban adorned with precious gems,
and his form was surrounded by thousands of millions of yakṣas.
Dedicated to bowing before Rudra, always intent on devotion to Rudra,
and ever engaged in the worship of Rudra, may he perform my rite of pacification.
Virūpākṣa, the lord of the yakṣas, was clothed in white garments and possessed great splendor;
adorned at all times with beautiful golden garlands accompanied by the tinkling of small bells, he was solely intent upon granting boons.
May Rudrapūjā, the supreme devotee, perform my rite of pacification.
The yakṣas who dwell in the intermediate space, the yakṣas who reside in heaven,
and the yakṣas who inhabit the earth in mountain caves and inaccessible strongholds.
The yakṣas dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), assuming various forms and raising their weapons,
were devotees of Śiva, well-disposed, and eager for the worship of Śiva.
May the Yakṣiṇīs of various forms, as well as the Yakṣa maidens— joyful, peaceful, and devoted to peace— grant me tranquility.
May the highly fortunate Yakṣa maidens, who are devoted to the worship of Śiva,
being ever composed, grant peace, auspiciousness, security, strength, wondrous (and supreme) well-being, and swift success.
All the mountains from every side, and the mountain-dwelling beings of great supernatural power.
May the devotees of Śiva always grant me well-being at all times;
and may all the oceans everywhere, as well as any others upon the earth, do the same.
May all the Rākṣasas everywhere, even those of terrible form, constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra, perform my propitiation.
Those Rākṣasas who possess great heroism, those Rākṣasas who possess great strength,
those Rākṣasas who dwell in heaven, and the Rākṣasas who are in the intermediate space;
May those Rākṣasas of the netherworld (Pātāla), who are constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra and perpetually imbued with the thought of Śiva, grant me peace forever.
May the splendor of that god, whose form is Bhairava and is smeared with the ashes of the deceased, always grant me peace.
Then there were yoginīs of great power, always resplendent in their attire,
as well as ḍākinīs of great supernatural might who assumed many different forms.
May those who are devoted to bowing to Rudra, who delight in the worship of Rudra’s form,
and whose minds are solely fixed on Rudra, perform my rite of pacification.
The ḍākinīs who have gone into the intermediate space, those residing in heaven,
those dwelling in the netherworld and on the surface of the earth, and those situated in mountain fastnesses— [all these were summoned].
May the third eye of that God, whose trident is radiant with ashes, always grant me peace through its splendor.
All beings were of great form; all beings were exceedingly radiant;
all beings remained gentle; all beings were as swift as thought.

And those beings who are in the intermediate space, those beings who are established beyond the beginning of existence, and the beings on the surface of the netherworld and the earth, who bestow knowledge of what exists and what does not exist;
May the splendor of that deity, whose hand-palms hold a stainless khaṭvāṅga and a trident, always grant me peace.
All the heroic hosts of pretas, those pretas who face in every direction,
those pretas who are exceedingly radiant, and those pretas whose faces are smeared with blood.
And those pretas who are in the intermediate space, those pretas who dwell in heaven,
the pretas in the netherworld and on the surface of the earth, and those pretas who can assume any form at will.
May the splendor of that god, whose abode is the cremation ground and whose vehicle is the bull, grant me peace at all times.
Those Piśācas who are of great heroism, possessed of supernatural powers, and of immeasurable radiance—
all of them assume various forms and are exceedingly virtuous.
Those Piśācas who are in the intermediate space, those Piśācas who are in heaven,
and those Piśācas on the surface of the earth— multiform and swift as thought.
May the splendor of that God— who has the crescent moon upon his head and who is adorned with ashes— always grant me peace.
All those possessed by the epilepsy-grahas, all those possessed by the fever-grahas,
those who are possessed by the grahas of the womb and children, and those possessed by various disease-grahas;

Those planets that are in the intermediate space, those excellent planets that are in heaven, those that are on earth and in the netherworld, and those planets that are in every direction within the house; [to them all, I bow].
May that god, whose throat is deep blue and whose ornament is a serpent, always grant me peace through his splendor.
Thus may all the gods and others, who impart the knowledge of Śiva,
always grant peace to the world and to the devotees of Śiva.
Victory to you who are established in the yoga of the Self; victory to you whose intellect is perfectly purified;
victory to you, the sole hero in generosity; homage be to you, the Lord of Victory!
Victory to the supreme deity! Victory to the bringer of auspiciousness!
Victory to the one whose form is manifest! Victory to you who are to be recited; salutations to you!
Salutations again and again to the Jina, who bestows the fortune of victory, who creates the splendor of triumph,
and whose speech is renowned throughout the world.
Victory to the one with the trident in hand; victory to the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff! Victory to the one whose form is unconquered; victory to You, O Form itself—homage to You!
Victory to you whose body is half that of your beloved; victory to you who wear the crescent moon!
Victory to you, the God of gods; obeisance to you, Mahādeva!
Victory to the Lord of the three worlds! Victory to the one of renowned fame!
Victory to the hero Śarva! Victory to Kīrti! Homage be to you!
Victory to you of the stainless body! Victory to you, the accomplisher of all aims!
Victory to you, the destroyer of Manmatha! Homage be to you, the Knower!
Whoever thus reads or even hears this chapter on pacification (śāntika),
having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One who desires a daughter obtains a daughter; one who desires victory obtains victory;
one who desires wealth obtains wealth; and one who desires a son obtains a son.
The seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge; the seeker of yoga attains yoga;
the pregnant woman obtains a son; and the maiden finds a virtuous husband.
Whatever desire a person here on earth prays for upon hearing this,
they shall quickly attain it all and become beloved by the gods.
Having heard and reflected upon this meritorious [account], a king should enter into battle;
having conquered his enemies, he shall be filled with auspicious blessings.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, his teaching unassailable;
he shall not be overcome by diseases, and he will be firmly established with sons and grandsons.
If a person recites this meritorious chapter on peace with a specific purpose in mind,
diseases arising from wind, bile, and other humors shall not afflict him.
For him there is no untimely death, nor is he bitten by any [creature];
poison does not affect his body, nor do dullness, blindness, or muteness occur.
He shall have no fear of calamities, nor shall there be fear of portents;
he shall never be tainted by the evil effects of malevolent incantations.
He who recites this day after day, his self fulfilled with all desires, shall always possess vigorous strength; there is no need to report anything to him that remains unknown.
One obtains here, by merely hearing it, ten million times the merit of all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, from every direction (especially so).
By hearing this, one obtains the fruit of ten Rājasūya sacrifices and a hundred Agniṣṭomas, multiplied millions upon millions of times over.
He shall be invulnerable to all the gods and especially to others;
free from all diseases, he shall live for more than a hundred years.
The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed,
the murderer of one who has sought refuge, and the betrayer of a trusting friend.
One who has committed grievous sins, such as being a slayer of father or mother,
is liberated from all those evils merely by hearing this.
This meritorious chapter on peace must not be given to anyone;
it was taught of old by Śiva that it should be given only to devotees of Śiva.
This merit should be bestowed by one desiring their own welfare upon those who recite it day after day for the sake of fulfilling all desires.
Thus ends the sixth chapter on Peace, together with the section on the fruits of the six-syllable worship and recitation of Śiva, in the Śivadharmaśāstra.
Then the seventh, Nandikeśvara, said:
"Those who always remember Īśāna and those who worship him..."
Those lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras) should be known as those who have fallen from the world of Rudra.
The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the Vedas, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—
none of these are worth even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
He who always worships Śiva is one who always performs sacrifices, always bestows gifts,
and always subsists on air alone.
To him who constantly worships Śiva or bows down to him with devotion,
Śiva, being pleased, bestows both yoga and liberation.
Whoever performs this worship for a month, eating but one meal a day and with senses subdued,
obtains a fruit that cannot be attained even by all the great sacrifices combined.
On the full moon day, the new moon day, as well as the fourteenth and eighth days [of the lunar fortnight],
one who bathes the Liṅga with water shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having fasted on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in honor of the Supreme Lord,
one should perform worship in the morning and at midday on the fourteenth day.
Having first drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the man who eats the sacrificial oblation while restraining his speech obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara on the occasion of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
one attains the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara resides.
The celibate student, having become pure, who worships Śiva at the three junctions of the day,
uplifts his family for seven generations and is glorified in the world of Śiva.

On the sacred festival days, one should worship Śiva with acts of charity, fasting, and observances, with offerings, vigils, and feasts, and according to the rites for the great ablution and other ceremonies.
Whatever merit one obtains from worshipping Śaṅkara for as long a period of time as it takes to reach a festival day,
that same merit one gains by worshipping on the festival day itself.
Therefore, on the auspicious festival days (parvan), one who desires to attain great merit should always worship Śiva with effort and according to the extent of one's wealth.
For six months in succession, one should worship Śaṅkara according to the prescribed rite.
One obtains all that very same merit from worshipping during the equinox;
this should be understood to be exactly the same during an eclipse and at the winter solstice.
On the intercalary days, at the sun’s passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), and at the commencement of the six-aśīti periods,
whatever merit is gained by worshipping Śaṅkara according to the prescribed rite over the course of four months— [that merit is obtained here].
One obtains that same merit by worshipping Śiva on the full moon day of Kārttika;
likewise, one obtains merit on the full moon days of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha.
Indeed, this four-month worship bestows the fruit of great merit;
he who, being diligent in the month of Māgha, worships Śiva at the three junctions of the day.
One shall obtain the merit of six months during the month of Māgha; of this there is no doubt.
As it is in Māgha, so it is in the month of Āṣāḍha and likewise in Kārttika.
The merit performed during these three months should be known as equal;
one obtains the merit of performing the Cāturmāsya rites through worship in the month of Puṣya.
The merit produced during the two months of Caitra and Phālguna shall be attained;
likewise, there is the fortnightly merit on the fourteenth day, the new moon day, and the full moon day.
The merit should be known as eightfold for one who worships Śiva on the eighth lunar day;
it is equal to that of one who gives a hundred thousand milch cows to a master of the Vedas.
The merit of one who worships the Liṅga for a single day is greater than that of a man who eats [only once] every month throughout his entire life.
And whoever should worship the Liṅga even once, this is equal [to the former], without a doubt;
know that by this sequential practice, the fruit is obtained day after day.
One should know that this applies even for a year; however, he who abandons social contact and worships Śiva for a full year [attains the highest result].
That merit increases a hundredfold through continuity;
for one who worships Śiva for half a year, that merit is increased fiftyfold.
In every season it should be half of that; in every month, half of that;
even he who worships the Liṅga continuously for half a month [attains the same].
The Supreme Person is to be known; for uninterrupted practice is indeed difficult.
He who, having risen in the morning, worships the Linga of Śiva with devotion— [is that person].
One who worships the Linga when the sun has reached its meridian shall obtain that same merit which is gained by giving a hundred Kapila cows.
One who properly worships Śiva when the sun has entered the constellation Vāruṇī (Śatabhiṣaj) shall obtain that merit which is gained by giving away the entire earth.
One who, having bathed and being pure, worships the Liṅga at midnight, shall obtain the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows.
He obtains, according to dharma, the fruit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices;
likewise, by worshipping Śaṅkara on the festival days at the proper times, as well as during his own [appointed] times.
A person who worships with devotion shall attain all desires;
for the Śiva-liṅga is of great merit and is saluted by all the gods.
Whoever constantly touches it is not defiled by sins;
they shall never again behold the perilous confusion of mixed births.
Those men who take refuge in the *liṅga* will gradually attain liberation,
even more so than by giving away all the earth along with Mount Meru made of gold.
They both worshipped that Liṅga, and as the fruit of that worship, even a heap of sinful deeds as large as Mount Meru or Mandara was [consumed]. They also offered oceans filled with food.
Just as a malignant disease is destroyed by resorting to a physician who is the Lord,
one who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva is freed from the consequences arising from great sins.
One would not be stained by the faults committed, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
even after cutting, piercing, and killing all these beings in this entire world.
One should worship the one Virūpākṣa; he is not defiled by sins,
even if he has fallen into any state whatsoever, and he goes to the supreme goal— even if he is joined with all manner of crimes.
Having worshipped Śiva, that man [should go] to the banks of rivers and oceans, to forests and groves, to lofty mountain peaks,
to caves and thickets, and to the vicinity of sacred fords and shrines.
Whether at a lotus pond or a lake, or wherever the mind finds delight, one should worship Śiva right there;
one will obtain the merit found in all sacrifices—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who, having abandoned the conceptualization of place, worships Śiva, obtains the entire fruit of the horse sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter.
One obtains here the entire fruit of the horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
This mass of merit is proclaimed as being attained even without the recitation of mantras.
This merit, when joined with a mantra, may be a hundred times greater.
Therefore, with a mantra, one should offer bathing water, perfumes, fruits, and so forth to Śarva.
One should offer land, cows, jewels, garments, and so forth, as well as oblations and other rites;
the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" should be known as the means for accomplishing all acts of worship.
And this six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Oṃ, is superior to all mantras;
for by Śiva, everything moving and unmoving has been pervaded both internally and externally.
Because it makes the entire world one, it is remembered as "Oṃ";
this [syllable] is sung with four morae (mātrās).
Brahmā, Hari, and Rudra are proclaimed to be its constituent parts (mātrās).
Brahmā is born from the right limb, and Hari arises from the left limb.
From the heart comes Nīlarudra, the awakener of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
Brahmā is the creator of the world, and Viṣṇu is the deluder of the worlds.
Brahmā is the creator of the world; Viṣṇu is the deluder of the worlds;
and Nīlarudra, whose essence is Śiva, is eternally intent upon bestowing grace.
The world is pervaded by these three causes, which are one's own actions;
these are the three measures (mātrās) of Śiva, worshipped by all the worlds.
These very three worlds, the three Vedas, the three fires,
the three qualities, the triple set of aims, and whatever else exists within the world [are all contained therein].
The half-measure is Parorudra, Śiva, the cause of causes;
from him this triad of causes of the world has arisen.
The Omniscient One is the cause, the pure, the great sacrifice of prostration;
therefore, one should worship Śiva through the self-sacrifice of prostration.
Ignorance constitutes non-Śiva-hood, since it is the abode of all suffering;
for that [non-Śiva-hood] is indeed attained through one's own nature, therefore Rudra is the Supreme Śiva.
Homage to Śiva, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes;
and having reflected, I offer myself again with a single-minded heart.
Having uttered "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," one is liberated from all sins;
therefore, one should recollect that mantra beginning with the syllable Oṃ.
At all times and in all activities, such as eating or spitting,
one should utter "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" and, having spoken the name of Śiva, attain the state of Śiva.
He who, while sleeping, waking, and at the time of death, remembers with constant mindfulness "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," shall go to the supreme goal.
Even a prostration offered to the wielder of the trident (Śiva) with deceit shall serve to loosen the thick bonds of cyclic existence.
Whether impure or pure, or even in whatever state one may be,
whoever remembers the Lord Īśāna is not defiled by sins.
Merely by remembering Rudra, the cage of the multitude of sins shatters into a hundred pieces,
just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
For the sake of the non-anger and the success of all devotees of Śiva,
Śiva spoke this mantra, which is the essence and the foundation for the fulfillment of all purposes.
The six-syllabled Śiva-sūtra is the true seed of all sciences, the primordial Brahman higher than the highest, the mantra that accomplishes all purposes.
The commentary on this very sūtra, concerning all the subsequent higher and lower knowledges, has been clearly expounded here by Śambhu.
Therefore, one should perform the worship of Śiva with this mantra;
and at the junction of day and night (sandhyā), one should recite it for the purification of all sins.
The merit at a water reservoir during the twilight is a hundred times that of being at home;
however, at the Southern Form of Śiva, that merit is ten thousand times greater.
Therefore, with a tranquil mind, one should perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā) in the abode of Śiva,
constantly using the Śiva-mantra for the accomplishment of all desires.
But he who worships [it] everywhere with special care and in great detail obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever worships him with devotion on the banks of rivers and oceans, in forests, or in groves, his merit is even greater than that.
For one who, with senses conquered and mind tranquil, worships with the Śiva-mantra,
his merit cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
It is impossible to say where he has gone, or in which country he might be dwelling.
Even that land would become purified; how much more so his kinsmen, from whom he eats food and who are his attendants?
For them also, because they are equal to that [state], there is no worship of Śiva without them here.
In that land where Śaṅkara is worshipped, there is no famine, nor does pestilence prevail; the king does not die an untimely death.
Whoever constantly worships Śiva, even if born of the lowest caste, provided they have conquered their senses and is endowed with such devotion, shall attain the supreme goal.
A student who has completed his vows is superior to thousands who have not;
one who has mastered the Vedas is superior to thousands of students who have completed their vows.
One who maintains the sacred fire is indeed superior to thousands of those who study the Vedas;
one who performs sacrifices is superior to thousands of those who maintain the sacred fire.
One who performs a *sattra* sacrifice is superior to thousands of performers of ordinary sacrifices;
one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge is superior to thousands of performers of *sattra* sacrifices.
One who knows the end of all sciences and is a devotee of Śiva is distinguished above all;
therefore, with a tranquil mind, one should worship Śiva in this manner with devotion.
He who is a devotee of Śiva, who has conquered anger, who is devoted to the knowledge of Śiva,
and who is friendly and compassionate, attains Sadāśiva.

One should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who abound in merit, sympathetic joy toward those endowed with merit, and equanimity toward those lacking merit; and one should speak of auspiciousness to everyone.
Having thus cultivated the mind in these five ways, one should worship Śiva,
having fully honored the Lord of Beings with a joyful inner self.
One should perform meditation as prescribed, which cuts away all sins,
after having worshipped the three-eyed Lord with supreme devotion.
Having joined his palms in reverence, a person should recite this hymn:
"Homage to you, whose form is knowledge, the sole cause of all knowledge!"
To you who are the essence of knowledge and discernment, eternally the supreme wisdom;
to you who are subtle, whose form is subtle, and who are the sole cause of subtle knowledge.
Salutations to You, the subtlest among even the subtle, the most minute of the minute; salutations to You, the divine, the divinely divine, the sole cause of the divine jewels;
salutations to You, the divine among even the divine, the most divine of all.
Salutations to you, the supreme one, the highest lord, the sole cause of the ultimate truth,
who are liberated from both the transcendent and the immanent, and who are most exalted.
Salutations to the one worthy of worship, to the one who is worshipful, to the sole cause of all that is worthy of worship;
salutations to the most worshipful one, who is the object of worship even for those who are themselves worshipped.
Salutations to the eternal one, whose form is eternal, who is the cause of the eternal enjoyment,
and who is the most eternal even among all things that are eternal.

Homage to the Radiant One, to the one more radiant than the radiant, to the sole cause of all radiance; homage to the one who is radiant even among the radiant, the source of the most intense radiance. Homage to the Essence, to that which has become the essence, to the sole cause of all essences.
Homage to the essence of even essences, to the most excellent essence;
to the Powerful One, who is the embodiment of power, the sole cause of all powers.
Salutations to the powerful among the powerful, to the most powerful of all;
salutations to the pure one, whose nature is purity, the sole cause of the purification of everything.
Salutations to the purest among the pure, to the most supremely pure;
to Time, who has the form of time, the sole cause of all time.
Homage to the Time of times, who has become the darkness of time;
homage to him whose body is all mantras, the sole cause of all mantras.
Homage to the mantra of mantras, homage to the most excellent of mantras;
homage again and again to Śāna, whose form is the measure of space.
Salutations again and again to the Puruṣa whose yoga has the sky as its measure;
salutations again and again to the Terrible One whose light has the sky as its measure.
Homage be to you, the Lord of the Left, who possesses the left-hand path as vast as space;
homage be to you, the Lord of Enjoyment, whose enjoyment is as vast as space.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Liberation, whose measure is the expanse of space, for the sake of liberation.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the universe, who pervades the entire world as far as the limits of space.
Homage to you who possess one body, two bodies, and many bodies;
homage again and again to the three-eyed one who is endowed with incalculable bodies.
Salutation to you who have one face, two faces, and many faces;
salutation to you, the Supreme Lord, endowed with innumerable faces.
Salutations to you who have one tongue, two tongues, and many tongues;
salutations again and again to you who are endowed with as many tongues as there are atoms, and who possess three eyes.
Salutations again and again to the Victorious One, whose truth is as vast as the sky.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of Desire, whose desires are as vast as the sky; salutations again and again to the Lord of the Divine, who is divine and immeasurable as the sky.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of Time, whose duration is equal to the measure of space; salutations again and again to the Lord of Dharma, whose nature is equal to the measure of space.
Salutations to you who have one tusk, two tusks, and many tusks;
salutations again and again to Tryambaka, who is endowed with a number of tusks beyond counting.
Salutations to you who have one throat, two throats, and many throats;
salutations to you, the blue-throated one, endowed with innumerable throats.
Salutations to you who have one hand, two hands, or many hands;
salutations always to you, Rudra, who possess innumerable hands.
Homage to you who have one eye, two eyes, and many eyes;
homage be to you, the Knower, who possesses innumerable eyes.
Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; salutations to you, O Maheśvara.
Salutations to you, O Mahāyogin; salutations to you, O Mahābala.
Salutations to you, the Great Lord; salutations to you, the Most Exalted;
salutations to you of great form; salutations to you, Sadāśiva.
Salutations to you, O Great Pure One; salutations to you, O Ever-Luminous One. Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; salutations to you, O Eternal Bhava.
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, Peaceful; salutations to you, O Blessed One, Eternal;
salutations to you, O Blessed One, Radiant; salutations to you, O Blessed One, Hara.
Salutations to you, O Unconquered One; salutations to you whose limbs are smeared with ashes.
Salutations to you, the Soul of All; salutations to you, the Lord of the Universe.
Homage to you, the All-Knowing; homage be to you, the All-Pervading.
Homage to you, the Infinite; homage again and again to you, the Lordless One.
Salutations to you, the unmanifest; salutations be to you, the eternal. Salutations to you, the one worthy of worship; salutations be to you, the bestower of boons.
Thus, whoever does not praise Maheśvara in this hymn,
having quickly abandoned all sins, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One seeking enjoyments obtains enjoyments; one seeking a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom;
one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; and one seeking yoga attains yoga.
The sick person is freed from diseases, the suffering person is liberated from suffering,
the bound person is released from bondage, and he who seeks glory shall obtain fame.
Whatever desires one contemplates, those very things one attains when cultivated;
that man who recites this constantly attains the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the Dharma of Giving, in the glorious Śivadharmaśāstra.
Then the eighth,
the illustrious Nandikeśvara, said: "Whatever holy fords and sacred shrines exist upon the earth,"
They dissolve into the *liṅga*; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*.
He who worships this most meritorious Liṅga, which grants the fulfillment of all aims, has bathed in all sacred fords and stands above all.
A *liṅga* established with a hundred [bricks] should not be moved even by a thousand;
whether it is poorly situated or well-situated, one must never move a *śivaliṅga*.
He who, being diligent, performs the ghee-consecration (*ghṛtābhiṣeka*) of Śiva for a full day and night with a small-mouthed jar during the month of Puṣya;
One should perform a vigil here, adorned with songs, dances, offerings, the sounds of conchs and musical instruments, and illuminated by lamps and other lights.
Freed from all sins, joined with his entire lineage,
fulfilled in all desires, and endowed with all virtues.
Endowed with blazing, equal, immeasurable, and unsurpassed great vehicles,
he rejoices eternally in the City of Śiva, happy like Śiva himself.
Whoever performs an ablution with ghee during an eclipse, at the equinoxes, or on auspicious days, shall attain great merit.
He who, having fasted for three nights, witnesses the consecration with clarified butter until its completion,
shakes off all sins and goes to the world of Śiva.
One person worships with devotion, and another perceives [the deity] with devotion;
the fruit for both of them is exactly the same, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Whoever should undertake the commencement of a great procession on festival days,
or the chariot procession of Śiva, or the circumambulation within the city;
With great variegated banners and parasols accompanied by the tinkling of small bells,
with canopies, garlands of flags, bells, chowries, and mirrors.
Amidst the tumultuous sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, crowded with songs, dances, and the like,
[there were] painted figures and wooden mechanical contraptions representing the hosts of Mothers, Rākṣasas, and others.
With many wonderful water-machines and fire-engines of various kinds,
and with circular swings for women, and great wheels suspended from eight points;
It was filled with oceans, lakes, wells, and other features, endowed with great sacrificial sessions,
crowded with large populations, and extended according to the full extent of its wealth.
The merit of all acts of giving, the fruits of all sacrifices,
the merit of those who perform most rigorous austerities, and the fruits of all sacred fords— [all these are attained here].
Having become free from disease and endowed with glory through the promotion of the pilgrimage to Śiva,
he rejoices for a long time in the world of Śiva, enjoying great pleasures like Śiva himself.
At the end of that [life], he shall attain the sovereignty of the king of gods for a very long time;
thereafter, he becomes a glorious lord of Jambūdvīpa, and finally, he becomes a sovereign of the earth.
He who gives a "blanket of ghee" as far as the Āliṅga altar attains these rewards.
The fruit of that [act] is like a stream of clarified butter on the full-moon festival in the month of Māgha.
One is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred Manvantaras;
by performing the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) correctly, one attains the world of Śiva,
and having descended from there, one is born here handsome, fortunate, and prosperous.
Having fashioned an image of form made of flour, with three eyes and adorned with jewels,
provided with a sacred thread and especially standing on one foot;
its teeth are of pearl, and its lower lips are of coral.
One should place a vajra upon the two eyes, or a lapis lazuli gem if the former is unavailable.
One should fashion [the image] of gold and silver with the two hands, and apply copper to the feet;
one should then wrap it with various cloths made from silk-worms or from foam.
One should also adorn it with fragrant flowers of various colors;
there, one should prepare an offering (bali) consisting of various kinds of food, both solid and soft.
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and satisfy the Brahmins with devotion;
having said, "May Śiva be pleased with me always," one should dismiss the twice-born.
Having brought that very form to the temple of Śiva along with those eminent Brahmins in great numbers,
he should worship it upon the altar in the vicinity of the Śiva-liṅga.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruits of all gifts,
one who gives the gift of beauty becomes handsome and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should offer food filled with ghee and adorned on top with honey,
as well as one Magadha-prastha measure of black sesame seeds.
One should cause two prasthas of rice to be given separately;
it should be wrapped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and new cloths.
One should also present an offering of all kinds of food and drink,
having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, especially on the full moon day.
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for ten thousand times ten thousand ages.
Upon the exhaustion of merit, having returned here, one is born into a prosperous family—
intelligent, fortunate, illustrious, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
having offered a copper vessel filled with water containing gold within it.
Having properly covered it with an upper lotus, honored it with perfumes and flowers, and having duly fed a great devotee of Śiva who is a twice-born according to the prescribed rite;
When the moon has risen in the east and the sun has set in the west,
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should place the domestic vessel before Śiva.
"May Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe in the form of Soma, be pleased with me. To that brahmin, he should then respectfully and slowly offer that vessel.
Having performed this vow known as Somavrata, one shall go to the presence of Rudra.
Upon descending from the world of Rudra, that man becomes one who remembers his past births;
through the force of his former practice, he shall once again proceed to the city of Śiva.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, having worshipped Śiva with effort (or devotion),
one who wears the sacred thread should give white [rice] and other offerings and feed the devotees of Śiva.
Furthermore, on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should worship Śambhu and ask for his forgiveness;
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the ascetics, adorned with threads, garments, and other such items.
Whoever performs this Cāturmāsya Pavitraka rite even once shall be honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Fallen from his state due to the exhaustion of merit, he is born as a knower of the four Vedas;
or, by his own will, he may become a king endowed with virtue and prowess.
Whatever merit belongs to the gift of land and whatever fruit belongs to the gift of a maiden—
by means of a wind instrument, a person obtains both of those merits.
That very same [merit] belongs to one who sings meritorious songs and especially to one who dances;
likewise, it belongs to one who utters the word "Victory! and to one who makes the sound of hand-clapping.
One should give a milch cow, young and accompanied by a bull, to Śiva; by that act, the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, becomes as if given.
One should offer a bull with fully developed limbs, noble and moon-bright,
or even a draft-ox capable of bearing the yoke, according to one's desire.
As many as are the hairs on his body and the lineages from which they were born,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Śiva.
With the intention of performing a ritual bath or a fire sacrifice, by giving a well-formed,
milch, noble-bred tawny cow, it becomes as if a hundred cows have been given.
Just as a mother protects her son from fearful wildernesses and difficult terrains, so too does the Kapila cow;
therefore, one should diligently offer a Kapila cow for the sake of auspiciousness.
The ghee of a Kapila cow has been produced for the purpose of rites such as the ritual bathing of Śiva;
therefore, one who desires the auspiciousness of the Kapila cow should employ it right there.

The Śūdra who, being devoid of the purificatory rites of Śiva, drinks from a *kapilā* [cow], goes to a most terrible hell filled with agonies. A Brāhmaṇa should drink the remnants of the oblation; otherwise, he is like a beast, even if he has the face of heaven.
Having bowed to Gaṅgā, whoever performs a circumambulation of her has thereby circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
Since sin is destroyed by the sound of the cows' *huṃkāra*, as well as by seeing and touching them, one should therefore behold and touch them.
For how could there be sins for those whose homes are adorned?
Those holy places on earth that extend everywhere as far as the ocean, which were constantly visited by cows with their calves like goddesses of fortune (Śrīs) themselves—
One does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit gained from bathing in the water from a cow's horn;
one should step over the bones of a cow, but never avoid one that is dead.
As long as one inhales that fragrance, for so long is one filled with merit;
by scratching the cows and offering incense, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
Protecting [beings] from fear, disease, and other afflictions is equal to the gift of a hundred cows;
so too is one who provides cattle and the like, furnished with grass, water, and other necessities.
He obtains merit equal to that of a horse-sacrifice; there is no doubt about this. What is the use of saying more? Cows must be protected with great effort.
Cows must always be protected from wretchedness, nourished, and never subjected to seizure;
those who strike them are sinners against the mothers of all the world.
Out of delusion, they cry out, "This world has been dragged away by them!
If a mortal should strike one, or if that lowest of men should revile him;
He would be cooked in the fire of hell, fanned by the breath of a cow; yet, when that fire is extinguished by a leafy branch, he brings about the destruction of his body.
She should say to her, "I am going," and she should not stop her, saying, "O Mother.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual release of the plough on both fortnights.
On the twelfth and fifteenth days, and on the fourteenth and eighth days as well—
O Viṣṇu, his cows, bulls, Śiva, Umā, and all the deities [are present].
Highly pleased, they bestow peace, heaven, long life, strength, and prosperity;
and they shall always and eternally grant what is auspicious and truly beneficial.
Thus, he who conducts himself toward cows avoiding beating and abuse attains great prosperity and goes to the world of Rudra.
If one who is striving for the sake of a cow or a Brahmin is deprived of life,
he attains the supreme abode where the Lord Maheśvara dwells.

The Brahmins and the cows constitute a single family divided into two parts; in one part reside the mantras, and in the other the sacrificial oblation (havis). Through cows the sacrifices proceed; in cows the gods are established.
The Vedas, along with their six auxiliary limbs, word-for-word commentaries, and phonetic arrangements, were brought forth by the cows.
At the base of the cows' horns, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed;
at the tips of their horns reside all sacred fords, both stationary and moving.
In the center of the head resides Mahādeva, the lord of all the gods.
The Goddess resides at the tip of the forehead; Ṣaṇmukha is in the bridge of the nose;
and the two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, are situated in the nostrils.
The two Aśvin deities reside in the ears; the Moon and the Sun in the eyes;
all the winds in the teeth; and Varuṇa is situated in the tongue.
Sarasvatī resides in the syllable *huṃ*; Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks;
likewise, the two twilights are in the two lips, and Indra has taken refuge in the neck.
The stars, the mountain peaks, and the heavens are situated upon his chest;
Dharma in its entirety, consisting of four feet, is himself well-established in his shanks.
The eleven Rudras are on its back, the Vasus are situated in its joints,
the Gandharvas are in the middle of its hooves, and the Pannagas are at the tips of its hooves.
The host of Apsarases stands at the rear tips of the hooves;
the eleven Rudras are on the back, and the Vasus are stationed at the joints.
The fathers reside upon the surface of the hips; the mothers are situated within the womb;
and the rays of the sun stand there as hairs, gathered together in a mass.
In his exhaled breath is the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves;
the Gaṅgā herself resides in his cow-urine, and the Yamunā in his cow-dung;
twenty-eight crores of deities dwell within the pores of his skin.
The four oceans are filled with the milk of cows;
all this has been told to you regarding how [the world] is established upon the cows.
That which is given, offered in sacrifice, or consumed—all that exists, both moving and unmoving—is contained within cows.
Therefore, cows must not be harmed; they should always be protected.
Cows are worthy of praise and worship; may cows protect me forever.
He who is praised by Brahmā with the word "Brahman" and by means of the *praṇava*—
that eternal Śiva shall forever ward off the enemy of the cattle.
May that eternal god Śiva, who is constantly worshipped with devotion by the powerful Viṣṇu, dispel the consumption of cattle.
May that eternal god Śiva, who is worshipped by the elephant-faced god Lambodara, drive away the affliction caused by Goṣumāri.
May that eternal god Śiva, who is worshipped even by the Sun, the remover of all diseases, dispel the Goṣumārī affliction.
He who is glorious and is constantly saluted with devotion by the Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa, whose body is radiant, with a joyful and single-minded heart.
May that eternal god Śiva dispel Goṣumārī;
may he thus dispel Goṣumārī accompanied by such calamities.
May the divine Ghaṇṭākarṇagaṇa, who is eternally endowed with the power of Rudra and possessed of Rudra’s energy, drive away Goṣumāri.
May the divine Ghaṇṭākarṇa Gaṇa, the bestower of the knowledge of Śiva,
dispel the consumption of cattle through the majestic power of Śiva.
Salutations always to Śiva, the God of gods, to Mahādeva, the radiant one; salutations to you, Rudra, Sthāṇu, Hara, and Ugra.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, the perfected one, the bestower of all accomplishments,
the three-eyed Maheśa, who is exceedingly peaceful.
Having consecrated this water with these mantras in their proper order, one should sprinkle the bodies of the cows; thereafter, peace will prevail.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious Gōsāvitrī, especially when cows are afflicted by disease, from that [recitation] peace shall arise.
Whoever, having risen, should constantly recite this *Gosāvitrī* at the time of releasing cattle, or during their departure or their gathering,
shall become long-lived, powerful, illustrious, possessed of cattle, and a lord of wealth.

And at the end of the Dohā, he shall go to the abode of Śiva; of this there is no doubt. May the cows, accompanied by bulls, graze daily upon abundant water and lush grass in the forests with healthy calves; may they yield milk happily and sleep in peace.
Whoever offers a supreme, well-adorned jackal,
he shall obtain eightfold the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Whether it be a well-disciplined woman or a man that one should present,
one shall obtain sixfold the fruit of the human-sacrifice (naramedha).
One should devoutly offer three elephants adorned with ornaments to Śiva on that auspicious day; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof.
He sports in many ways with hundreds of magnificent great vehicles, yoked to intoxicated elephants resembling Airāvata.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and tens of millions of kalpas, one shall dwell in the world of Rudra; thereafter, at the end, one shall become Indra, the lord of the gods.
He who provides water for the sacrifice to Śiva shall become glorious like Indra, endowed with beauty, heroism, and strength, and [he shall possess] land where all crops grow.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of that lord of the earth who should give the earth as a gift.
As many daṇḍas as the earth would measure when measured all around, for that many kalpas he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In this manner, the extent of the offense should be understood everywhere according to the measure of the punishment;
one should report whether it concerns a village, a hamlet, a city, a field, a district, or the like.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives a village endowed with all kinds of crops and fruits, and free from all afflictions, to Śiva.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices,
and whatever merit is found in all acts of giving— that shall be obtained by the gift of a village.
Resembling ten million suns and accompanied by ten million celestial women.
For hundreds of millions of eons, they shall be endowed with all objects of desire.
By the gift of a village with its celestial palaces (*vimāna*), one, together with seven times three generations of his kin,
sports at will in the world of Īśvara for imperishable time.
The merit of the gift of a city is a hundred times greater than that of the gift of a village.
Even by the gift of the entire earth, its infinity cannot be fully proclaimed.
All jewels, food, drink, cattle, horses, and mountains are produced from the earth;
therefore, one obtains the fruit of all gifts by the gift of land.
Yet, that man who seizes land—whether given by another or given by himself—[incurs great sin].
He is cooked in the hells for an inexhaustible period of time, one after another.
Everything has indeed been taken away by the seizure of land; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the seizer of land shall remain in the hells until the destruction of the earth.
Those men who, fearless of hell, here seize the property of the gods and the property of Brahmins out of delusion, are cooked in the hells.
O King, the mounts of the lord of the earth, nourished by the property of Brahmins,
will not endure at the time of battle, just like embankments made of sand.
One who bestows land shall dwell in heaven for a period measured by that number;
however, having seized it, one shall dwell in hell for a period a hundred times longer than that.
O Lord, those who steal the property of a Brahmin are cooked in succession within the twenty-eight most dreadful millions of hells.

Having emerged from their ends at the conclusion of time, they wander for a very long duration through births such as those of trees and insects, tormented by hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions.
Thus they wander for a very long time, subsisting upon the Lord,
until [they are rescued] by some devotee of Śiva in the temples and other sacred places of Śiva.
Then, by that fierce splendor, the thief’s own self was shaken off.
They go to heaven, having cast off this body consisting of suffering.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Fruit of Bestowing [Gifts] upon Śiva," in the glorious Śivadharmaśāstra.
Now begins the ninth [chapter].
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
O best of sages, hereafter I shall describe this meritorious [account],
which is endowed with supreme merit and practiced by all the gods.
[By Varuṇa, Āditya, Soma, Agni, Marut, Dhanañjaya, and Nārada;
by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Goddess, Skanda, Indra, and Yama;
[by Varuṇa, Āditya, Soma, Agni, Marut, Dhanañjaya, and Nārada.]
The constellation Śukra, the glory of Dharma, was eclipsed by Śanaiścara,
along with Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Budha, and the others.
[He was accompanied] by Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīca, and all the preeminent sages,
as well as by Bhṛṅgin, Mātṛ, Mahākāla, Caṇḍeśvara, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
By Vṛṣa, Vāsuki, Kārkoṭaka, Gulika, Ananta,
Takṣaka, Padma, Śaṅkha, Mahāpadma, and other great serpents as well.
[What need is there for] Siddhas, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, or the high-souled Vasus; nor even for Apsarases, Daityas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, or hosts of Bhūtas?
Just as the auspicious state of existence, which surpasses all other states,
was attained by me through the grace of the Lord, so now hear the supreme method.
Having bathed the liṅga with water scented with white sandalwood and having smeared it [with unguents],
one should worship it with white, blooming lotuses and prostrate before it.
In the midst of a pure, gentle, unblemished, flowering, and white lotus,
one should duly install a small, auspicious liṅga made of all fragrances, measuring only the size of a thumb, within the mass of filaments.
Having established [the deity] in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should worship him with bilva leaves;
one should offer agarwood on the right side, realgar on the west,
sandalwood on the north, and yellow orpiment on the east.
One should worship with fragrant and variegated flowers;
and having offered incense, either black agallochum or guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
One should offer very fine garments with their fringes intact,
and one should cause milk-rice mixed with ghee and ghee-lamps to be presented.
Having offered everything with the *nivedya* mantra, one should then perform a circumambulation;
having prostrated with the head before the Lord of Gods, one should rise at the end and ask for forgiveness,
offering that *liṅga* together with all the ritual offerings.
For the sake of Śiva, having taken refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti with the Śiva-mantra.
By this rite, O gods, all have attained divinity;
the Goddess attained her divine state, and Guha attained the state of Skanda.
Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā, and Hari attained the state of Viṣṇu;
likewise, he who constantly worships this Liṅga composed of all fragrances even once [attains the same].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
This is the supreme, secret vow, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga.
This has been declared to you, my devotee; it must not be given to just anyone.
Whoever removes the long-stale garland from Śiva— [he shall attain the fruit].
There is no doubt that he obtains the fruit of giving away a thousand cows.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Great Vow of the Liṅga," in the Śrī Śivadharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ten.
Nandikeśvara said:
On the fourteenth and likewise on the eighth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, [one should worship].
He who, being pure and devoted to the worship of Śiva, does not eat for one year;

Whatever inexhaustible merit is proclaimed for those who constantly perform sacrifices at night; whatever merit belongs to those established in truth and other virtues; whatever merit belongs to those who approach their wives during the proper season; whatever merit belongs to the maintainer of the sacred fire; and whatever merit belongs to those who perform Vedic sacrifices.
All that merit of his goes to the world of Śiva;
having made the earth his vessel, he has eaten with diligence on the sacred festival days.
By means of a single day and night, a man obtains the fruit of three nights;
likewise for two fifth days and two first days (pratipad) of the month.
Fasting and perfumed, he should lie down with his beloved;
yet he should sleep with a steady mind, devoid of carnal passion or worldly attachment.
And for one whose habit is the constant recollection of Śiva, hear now the fruit of his merit:
for a thousand divine years and likewise a hundred divine years.
By him great austerity has been performed; this shall undoubtedly come to pass.
Even if one who is deeply devoted to Śiva and whose soul is well-pleased should be a doer of evil deeds,
he shall dwell eternally in the world of Śiva, surrounded by the Gaṇas like Śiva himself.
By observing a fast at night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one attains enjoyment in this world and an auspicious state in the hereafter.
He who, for one year, observes the practice of eating only at night on every lunar festival day,
remaining celibate, conquering anger, and devoted to the worship of Śiva and the recitation of prayers;
At the end of the year, having fed the foremost of Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva with concentrated devotion, he should then say: "May the Blessed Lord Śiva be pleased."
O Lord of Gods, he who feeds a learned man observing the Kapāla vow has thereby fed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Whoever accepts alms-food filled in a skull-bowl from another person uplifts that person's lineage,
including ten ancestors and ten descendants.

Having seen the observer of the vow, one should honor him on all sides with water for the feet, water for respectful offering, water for sipping, and with perfumes and flowers; thereafter, one should satisfy him with alms-food.
When they are honored, Śiva himself is directly honored; there is no doubt about this.
When they are insulted, the Supreme Lord himself is indeed insulted.
Whatever one gives in an alms-bowl endowed with supreme purity, that gift bears fruit for him; it shall go forth a hundred thousandfold.
Thus, endowed with this ritual procedure, he goes to the world of Śiva;
that man shall not again attain the unstable world of mortals.
Alms are superior to fasting; unasked food is superior to alms;
eating at night is superior to unasked food; therefore, one should subsist by eating at night.
The gods partake of their portion in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday,
the ancestors in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others during the twilight.
Transcending all times, the supreme meal is at night;
Mahādeva, who follows the left-hand path, uplifts men by means of the nocturnal meal.
One should practice eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in diet,
performing fire-rituals, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.

Having diligently observed the night-vow (nakta) according to the prescribed rules on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should indeed worship Śaṅkara in this manner.
Having drunk cow's urine according to one's capacity while fasting, one should sleep during the night;
thus, one shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship the deity named Māheśvara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
by drinking cow’s milk at night, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices.
Likewise, having worshipped the Lord named Śambhu during the month of Pauṣa,
and consuming clarified butter on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains the merit of eight Vājapeya sacrifices.
Having drunk cow’s milk at night, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices;
and in the month of Phālguna, having worshipped Mahādeva, one should consume sesame seeds.
One shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
and in the month of Caitra, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Sthāṇu.
By eating roasted barley grains, one obtains the merit of eight horse sacrifices (aśvamedhas).
Having worshipped the deity named Śiva during the month of Vaiśākha and drinking water infused with kuśa grass at night,
one obtains eightfold the fruit of a human sacrifice (puruṣamedha).
Having worshipped Paśupati in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink water from the horns of cows;
one shall thereby obtain the fruit that results from the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, having worshipped the one named Ugra and consumed cow-dung,
one obtains eightfold the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. In Śrāvaṇa, having worshipped the one named Śarva, one should consume arka at night.
One is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred divine crores of years;
on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Īśvara.
Having drunk rice-water at night while offering fragrant flowers,
one shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
In the month of Kārttika, having worshipped the one named Rudra, one should consume curd;
thus one obtains eightfold the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva,
[offering] milk-rice mixed with ghee and well-sprinkled with honey.
According to one's capacity, one should offer gold and garments to them with devotion;
and one should offer a black, milch cow to Rudra.
Listen to the meritorious fruit for that man who performs the vow known as Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī in this manner continuously for one year:
he shall be completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all forms of sovereignty.
He shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva and never return here again;
for this is true regarding all meritorious occasions, such as the equinoxes and lunar eclipses.
The merit arising from acts such as giving, fasting, and fire-offerings becomes exhausted;
therefore, I shall describe each month the unsurpassed Śiva-vrata.

For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, for embodied beings such as men and women, whoever— having conquered the senses and speaking the truth— observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Puṣya has arrived, [should subsist] on rice, wheat, and dairy products.
Therefore, one should pass the eighth day of both fortnights by fasting;
one should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual with devotion.

At the end of the month, on the full moon day, having slept upon the ground and performed a bath with ghee and other substances, one should perform a great worship, enacting it with the mantras of Śiva.
One should offer as a food offering (naivedya) a prastha of barley-gruel and prepared milk;
furthermore, one should feed eight Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should give a pair of Śiva and Śivā, or one should offer a tawny cow that is well-adorned and beautiful; hear now the fruit of his merit.
With celestial chariots resembling ten million suns, accessible everywhere,
crowded with Rudra-maidens, and yoked with great bulls.
Adorned by hosts of apsarases with songs, dances, and instrumental music,
he was fanned with yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras.
Three-eyed and trident-handed, endowed with the sovereignty of Śiva,
he went to the divine city of Śiva where Śaṅkara himself resides.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are hairs on that [image], one shall dwell happily in the city of Śiva within the families born from it.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with twenty-one families,
and having attained the yoga of knowledge, one is liberated right there.
Through yoga one attains the end of suffering; from knowledge, yoga proceeds.
Knowledge arises from the Śiva-dharma, and the Śiva-dharma comes from the worship of Śiva.
Thus has been fully explained to you this means for attaining the liberation of Śiva, for those who abide in the ocean of saṃsāra and are devoted to the worship of Śiva.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming kṛsara mixed with ghee while his senses are restrained;
One should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights;
however, on the full moon day, a "blanket of ghee" (ghṛtakambala) should be offered to Śiva.
One should also present here a beautiful pair of black cattle;
having performed the remainder as prescribed, one obtains the fruit mentioned previously.
Having traveled in celestial chariots resembling sapphire and accompanied by peacocks to the beautiful city of Śiva, they shall enjoy their desired pleasures.
