When the month of Phālguna has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night— conquering anger and subduing the senses— with śyāmāka grain, milk, and nīvāra rice;
On the fourteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight, one should be devoted to fasting;
on the full moon day, a great ablution should be performed with the five products of the cow, ghee, and other substances.
With earth from the top of an anthill and so forth, with cow urine, cow dung, and the like,
with the barks of milk-exuding trees, and with metallic minerals, fragrant substances, and so on,
one should devoutly present a pair of copper-colored cows to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having performed the remaining other rites as prescribed, one obtains a great fruit.
Having traveled in celestial chariots resembling rubies that follow the path,
one goes to the beautiful city of Śiva and attains the qualities previously mentioned.
When the auspicious month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming nourishing food mixed with milk while his senses are restrained;
In this rite, one should offer a pair of cows, a *pāṭala* bull well-adorned and handsome, to Śiva; the remainder of the procedure should be performed as previously described.
At the end of his life, the self-controlled one goes to the supreme abode like Śiva,
[seated] upon [a throne] resembling clear pearls and adorned with sapphires.
When the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night shall travel in most delightful celestial chariots accompanied by Jīvas and Jīvakas.
Eating rice mixed with milk while his senses are restrained,
sleeping in a cow-pen, meditating on Śiva, and wearing only a single garment during the night.
One should practice all the general rules of discipline as they have been prescribed;
[one shall dwell] in celestial palaces resembling sapphires that fulfill all desires.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva, he rejoices for imperishable time.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform a ritual bath with ghee and other substances.
One should give a white, auspicious pair of cows along with a temple for Śiva;
[the donor] shall be adorned with celestial chariots resembling swans, jasmine flowers, and the moon.
Mounted upon a very white bull, surrounded by women endowed with every excellence, he proceeds to the abode of Śiva.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night shall sport for an inexhaustible time with women fragrant as blue lotuses.
Having washed śāli rice with milk and combined it with goat’s milk, one should fast for half the night;
during the day, one should follow after a cow.
Always acting for the benefit of cows and free from egoism,
he should perform the previously mentioned ritual of bathing and so forth on the full moon day.
In this rite, a pair of smoky-colored cows should be given as a gift,
adorned and accompanied by incomparable great vehicles resembling the petals of blue lotuses.
He who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, sports for an inexhaustible time with those bound upon great lions.
One should eat groats mixed with sugar-candy, clarified butter, and milk products;
and one should offer a pair of white cows, adorned and auspicious, to Śiva.
One should perform all the general rites previously enjoined,
[visualizing the deities] in vehicles resembling pure crystal and drawn by swans.
Endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest, he shall move about like Śiva;
so it is for one who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, one should offer a meal of milk and sixty-day rice,
as well as a white-tipped Pāṇḍu-pauṇḍra fruit and a pair of cattle to Śivā.
One should perform the entire general procedure as it has been proclaimed,
[proceeding] with various and wonderful great vehicles that have been arranged in diverse ways.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva, he obtains the aforementioned qualities;
this applies to one who performs the practice of eating only at night during the month of Bhādrapada.
Eating the remnants of the oblation offered in the fire, dwelling at the foot of a tree during the day,
and sleeping in a sanctuary at night, he should be compassionate toward all living beings.
One should offer to Śiva a bull with blue shoulders and horns adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli that shine like the rays of the sun.
Having traveled in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and are adorned with ruddy geese,
they go to the divine city of Śiva, which is worshipped by gods and asuras.
Possessing great splendor, he enjoys pleasures until the dissolution of all beings—
he who observes the practice of eating only at night in the glorious month of Āśvayuja.
Consuming ghee, with a serene soul and senses subdued,
[he should visualize] a bull, dark-blue in color like the neck of a peacock, with its chest elevated.
Having been liberated, he should now give a single cow, well-adorned, to Rudra;
he should perform the remainder of the ritual in its entirety, as previously described.
At the end of his journey, the self-controlled one goes to the abode of Śiva like Śiva himself,
traveling in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble pure pearls.
Accompanied by living Jīvaka birds and adorned with sapphires,
one goes to the auspicious city of Śiva and attains the qualities previously mentioned.
He who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika—
consuming food mixed with milk, speaking the truth, and having his senses subdued— shines with splendor.
One should also give a pair of cows, tawny-brown like a blazing fire;
by performing the previously mentioned rite, one shall become equal in virtue to Śiva.

In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night travels like Śiva himself, self-controlled, upon delightful Great Vehicles that resemble the crests of the fire at the end of an aeon and display the majestic stride of a great lion.
Eating barley-gruel mixed with milk, he should keep his senses restrained.
One should give a divine pair of white cows, well-adorned;
one should perform the entire previously mentioned procedure for Śiva.
Having traveled by means of vehicles resembling white lotuses and yoked with excellent white horses,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva and become equal in power to Śiva himself.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, tranquility,
bathing three times a day, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
"One should observe fasts on the fourteenth and eighth days of both lunar fortnights"—
one should not practice such rules directed toward Śiva.
A woman who is a devotee of Śiva will certainly become a man.
If she desires even the highest state of womanhood, listen to that vow called Umāmaheśvara, which eternally increases love.
It brings about non-separation, is peaceful, and accomplishes the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha;
[this should be practiced] on the full moon, the new moon, and on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
For a year, she should observe celibacy and eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night.
Having fashioned a very beautiful golden image of Umā and Maheśvara,
or one made of silver, at the end of the year, he should bathe it with ghee and other substances.
Having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, with pairs of most beautiful garments,
and with all kinds of foods— both solid and soft— as well as canopies, banners, and chowries;
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and provide sustenance (or offer libations) to the poor and the helpless;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity, one should ask Śiva for forgiveness at the conclusion.
Having prepared a vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or the like, covered with a white cloth,
one should place an image within it as the central shrine.
Carrying that vessel upon his head, adorned with a canopy and an umbrella,
he should lead it to the temple of Śiva with the splendor of banners, conchs, and other regalia.
One should offer this vow to Maheśa in his form as the Liṅga;
one should place upon its altar a vessel endowed with beauty of form.
Then, having circumambulated and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
having thus completed the meritorious vow, one should hear [the account] until the fruit is obtained.
In the world of Īśvara, he rejoices together with the Rudras, traveling in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble the twelve suns, according to his wish.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
at the end of that time, she is honored in the world of Viṣṇu with great enjoyments.
Then, by the remainder of that karma, endowed with all desired objects,
she shall reach the world of Brahmā and attain supreme bliss.
Fallen from the world of Brahmā, she is honored like the Goddess Śrī herself;
revered by the worlds, she attains the realm of Prajāpati.
Having enjoyed pleasures and the happiness of those [sensual] delights, one shall dwell happily in the world of Soma;
from the world of Soma, having reached the world of Indra once more, one shall obtain Indra as a lord.
Having attained the Gandharva realm from the world of Indra,
she rejoices together with the lord of the Gandharva kings, enjoying manifold pleasures.
Having reached the wondrous world of the Yakṣas, which is adorned with blazing lights from great jewels, he rejoices there according to his desire.
Fallen from the world of the yakṣas, she sports on the summit of Mount Meru;
having arrived in turn at the abodes of the world-protectors, she rejoices.
Throughout the entire circle of the earth, as far as the limits of light and darkness,
wherever there may be divine happiness, may he obtain it all without exception.
Thus, having enjoyed all desired pleasures in all the worlds,
she will gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
Having obtained such a youth— one endowed with beauty, the lord of the entire earth, and a knower of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation— one rejoices.
Then, through the remainder of her merit, she becomes permeated by the Lord;
and due to the connection with the latent impressions of her own past actions, she again undertakes auspicious deeds.
Furthermore, from the auspicious state as well, one proceeds in this manner through thousands of future births;
as long as one does not attain world-weariness, one wanders on by means of karma.
As long as there is discernment, there is dispassion; from dispassion arises knowledge;
from knowledge yoga proceeds; and from yoga one attains the end of suffering.
On the eighth and fourteenth days [of the lunar fortnight], she who is self-restrained and observes celibacy shall not eat for one year, desiring to attain great enjoyment.
At the end of the year, having fashioned an image, one should perform the ritual as prescribed before;
having completed that vow beginning with the ablutions, she obtains the qualities previously mentioned.
Having traveled by means of celestial vehicles made of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with four gates,
one shall reach the divine city of Śiva and attain imperishable enjoyment.
Having enjoyed all desired pleasures in Śiva and all other worlds,
she shall gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
She who fasts for one year on a single day of the dark fortnight shall obtain a husband.
One who has committed [this] should fast for one year on the single fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
at the end of the year, having fashioned an auspicious image made of rice-flour, [he should worship it].
One should worship with yellow unguents, garlands, and yellow garments;
having performed everything previously mentioned, one should offer it to Śiva.
[The devotee shall ascend] great vehicles with seven stories, possessing the luster of molten gold.
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas.
Having enjoyed all desired pleasures in Śiva and all other worlds,
she shall return in due course to this world and obtain a husband according to her wish.
Restraining oneself well, one should remain without food on the new moon day for an entire year;
at the end of the year, having fashioned a trident out of flour,
one should offer it to Śiva, along with a silver lotus with a pericarp made of gold.
Having placed [the remainder] upon its head with devotion, one should perform the rest as previously described.
Whatever sin has been committed even out of desire, such as the killing of an embryo and so forth—
a woman shall undoubtedly destroy all of that by the gift of a trident.
In the Mahāpadma celestial mansion, crowded with men and women,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas;
having enjoyed desired pleasures in the worlds beginning with the realm of Śiva.
Having reached this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband.
Firm in her vow, she should fast on the full moon day for one year;
at the end of the year, she should offer an image enriched with all kinds of perfumes.
By means of beautiful, diverse, and auspicious Great Vehicle chariots made of divine fragrance,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas;
having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in the world of Īśvara as long as he desires.
Having come in due course to this world, she shall obtain a king as her husband—
she who passes the auspicious month of Kārttika by eating but one meal a day.
Endowed with restraints such as forbearance and non-violence, and remaining celibate,
she should offer oil-cake mixed with molasses and clarified butter at the end of each month.
On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], she should be devoted to fasting.
In celestial chariots resembling sapphire and fulfilling all desires,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years;
having obtained enjoyments in every respect throughout all the worlds as they truly are.
Having arrived in this world in due course, one shall obtain whatever one desires.
Thus, the procedure for all months is proclaimed to be the same;
and the wise know that the fruit of fasting by eating only one meal is identical [to that of the monthly fasts].
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of Śiva, fire-sacrifice, contentment, and the cultivation of non-stealing.
This general dharma for all vows is traditionally taught as tenfold;
I shall now also explain the specific rules regarding each monthly vow.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should adorn a bull made of flour with perfumes and garlands and offer it to Śiva.
By means of great vehicles yoked with bulls and endowed with excellent enjoyments,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having attained abundant happiness among all the hosts of gods,
she will gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.

In the month of Pauṣa, having placed the Pināka bow adorned with perfumes and garlands in a vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or other such materials, one should offer it to the wielder of the Pināka.
By means of the great Puṣpaka vehicle, which wafts divine fragrances,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures arising from all the cities, he [returns].
Having thus attained these worlds in succession, she shall obtain a husband according to her desire.
Having prepared a chariot yoked with horses, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
and equipped with a liṅga made of flour, one should bring it to the sacrificial ground.
By means of vehicles resembling great chariots and yoked with excellent white horses,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having obtained all desired enjoyments among all the classes of immortals,
she shall eventually come to this world and obtain a husband according to her wish.
In the month of Phālguna, having fashioned an image made of flour mixed with ghee and adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should install it in the temple of Īśvara.
By means of incomparable divine vehicles accompanied by song and dance,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than ten thousand years.
Having obtained enjoyments that are extremely difficult to find even among all the classes of immortals,
once she has reached this world in due course, she shall obtain a husband according to her desire.
Having fashioned an image of the youth Kumāra out of flour and adorned it,
one should place it in a vessel as prescribed and measure [the distance] toward the temple of Śiva.
In celestial palaces resembling the autumnal moon and fulfilling all desires,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of her karma, accompanied by sons and grandsons,
she obtains her desired husband and attains enjoyments that are very difficult to acquire.
Having fashioned Mount Kailāsa out of a measure (āḍhaka) of ground rice,
adorned with all minerals, and joined with Īśvara and Umā;
One should place [the image] in the temple of Īśvara, filled with various caves (or perforations) and joined with a prastha of salt, and endowed with all kinds of gems.
She who performs this Kailāsa-vrata in the month of Vaiśākha is honored in the world of Śiva with palaces resembling Mount Kailāsa.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with Śiva,
he returns in due course to this world and rejoices for a long time on the king of mountains.
Having fashioned a linga out of flour according to the Vedic rites during the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should worship it with devotion using perfumes and other offerings, and wrap it in a pair of garments.
One should perform the vigil there with special decorations; having led [the deities] into each vessel along with their respective offerings, one should place them in the sanctuary.
In celestial palaces resembling pure crystal that fulfill all desires,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for ten thousand times ten million divine years.
Having enjoyed all pleasures arising from every city according to her desire,
she will gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
Furthermore, by fashioning a seven-storied house out of flour in the month of Āṣāḍha...
It was filled with the essence of all seeds, possessed auspicious characteristics,
and was equipped with household utensils such as mortars, pestles, and the like.
With all kinds of jewels and other items, such as female servants and decorated beds;
with all these made of flour, adorned with lamps and the like;
provided with all kinds of edible foods, and decorated with perfumes and garlands.
It is adorned with banners and cloths of black, red, white, and yellow,
and is provided with the four kinds of sacrificial porridge as well as all types of grains.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, having placed the house before Śiva,
equipped with all its furnishings, one should prostrate and announce it to him.
For more than a hundred million years, he is honored in the world of Śiva by means of Mahāyāna vehicles of seven stages, overflowing with all enjoyments.
Having enjoyed vast and unsurpassed pleasures in all the worlds,
he attains on earth a seven-storied mansion enriched with every luxury.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer to Śarva a mountain of sesame seeds, strewn across its entire extent and adorned with various banners.
In magnificent, incomparable, and auspicious vehicles resembling clear sapphire,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred divine millions of years.
Having enjoyed various pleasures according to her heart's desire, she will,
in due course, reach this world again and obtain a king as her husband.
Having fashioned a beautiful mountain of rice in the month of Bhādrapada,
adorned with gold and cloth, one should offer it to Śiva.
With great vehicles adorned with paintings and provided with all enjoyments,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred million years.
Having enjoyed various pleasures arising from many cities,
she will eventually come to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
And having fashioned a vast mountain of grain in the month of Āśvayuja,
one should offer it, together with gold and garments, to Śiva.
In beautifully variegated great vehicles, endowed with excellent enjoyments,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of millions of years.
Having enjoyed pleasures according to her desire in the worlds beginning with the realm of Rudra,
she shall reach these worlds in succession and obtain a king as her husband.
Endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches, possessed of the essence of all seeds, joined with all minerals, and adorned with every kind of gem;
it was furnished with four peaks and beautified by canopies and parasols.
It was adorned with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps,
and resounded with various songs and melodies from conch shells, lutes, and other instruments.
It was accompanied by the sacred sounds of the Vedas and especially by meritorious auspicious recitations;
it was equipped with eight great banners and adorned with various flowers.
One should place the supreme king of mountains named Meru, the support of the three worlds,
and upon its summit, one should establish Śiva accompanied by all the gods.
And by the Daityas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas, as well as by hosts of Suras and Bhūtas,
by Vidyādharas, Apsarases, and Nāgas, and especially by the Ṛṣis.
The wise practitioner should fashion all the forms out of rice flour;
in the right hand of the deity should be a trident worshipped by the thirty gods.
In this manner, one should apply the weapons to all the deities in their proper sequence.
One should perform a grand worship of Śiva accompanied by the caru offering;
one should worship all the gods and present the bali offering in the ten directions.
One should feed all the twice-born who are devotees of Śiva, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
as well as other initiated practitioners, those observing vows, and spiritual adepts (sādhakas).
With the permission of the preceptor, the virtuous woman should bow to Meru as it stands present,
fully prepared with all its undertakings and arranged according to the extent of her wealth.
One should offer the supreme Kārttikagama to Rudra;
listen now to the fruit of merit for her who performs this even once.
Whatever merit has been described by the sages of old in all the scriptures,
she shall obtain that merit multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt.
By means of vehicles possessing the luster of great jewels, endowed with all desirable objects,
adorned with dancing, singing, instrumental music, and attended by hosts of apsarases.
With celestial chariots resembling Mount Meru, radiant as ten million suns,
filled with men and women, auspicious, and wafting divine fragrances;
Being praised by the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and the lords of the hosts, she,
having become independent and omnipresent, proceeded to the abode of Īśvara.
That woman of great austerity rejoices for a hundred divine millions of kalpas;
thus, having enjoyed all desired pleasures in every world, she remains.
O protector of the earth, having returned here due to the exhaustion of her merit, she shall become his beloved;
she will always be beautiful, fortunate, and devoted to her lord.
Whatever purpose men, women, or eunuchs have in mind when they worship Śiva with devotion, that very thing is swiftly accomplished.
Having constructed a house or even a temple made of clay, wood, stone, or flour, according to one's means and with well-executed craftsmanship.
Having thus given a house equipped with all necessaries and filled with all kinds of grain to Śiva, one shall obtain all desires.
Having spoken thus, she remained well-restrained for one month during the winter season, eating only a single meal a day;
and at the end of the month, she had a chariot constructed, adorned with variegated cloths.
It was yoked to four white bulls,
beautifully adorned with banners, sacrificial posts, and the like, as well as umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors;
having fashioned a Vedic *liṅga* from a measure (*āḍhaka*) of ground rice, he [proceeded].
Having placed [the image] in the middle of the chariot, one should worship it according to the prescribed characteristics;
then, during that night, one should proceed along the path of the chariot with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Having slowly circumambulated [the sacred site], one should thereafter proceed to the temple of Śiva.
There, with vigils and worship adorned by lamps and other offerings,
and by the offering of consecrated water (*prokṣaṇīya*), one should gradually spend the night.
At dawn, having performed the ritual bathing and provided food for his devotees,
he gave sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability to the poor, the helpless, and the blind.
One should offer [the image] adorned with the splendor of a chariot for the sake of Śiva.
Having eaten together with one's kinsmen and having bowed to the Lord, one should return home.
Among all vows, this is supreme; herein dharma is fully accomplished.
The vow named Śivaratha is the accomplisher of all desires and goals.
Whatever merit exists in all vows and whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices—
all that shall indeed be attained as the fruit of merit by one who is devoted to the chariot of Śiva.
Together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva by means of celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble ten thousand suns.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in all the worlds in succession for more than ten million times ten thousand eons, at the end of that eon, he [becomes] a lord of the earth.
She obtains a husband who is young, endowed with beauty, possessed of enjoyments, ever virtuous, a king, and eager for pleasure;
she also obtains a most beautiful bed, soft and provided with five layers of cotton.
One should prepare an auspicious bed equipped with all necessary articles; having fashioned an image of Śiva together with the Goddess out of flour, one should offer it upon this bed.
Having honored with humility the preceptor— who knows the meaning and reality of the knowledge of Śiva— with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as garments, ornaments, chowries,
and all kinds of edible foods, one should then offer a bed.
There, for as many thousands of years as there are individual fibers in wool or cotton, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with Śiva,
he shall gradually return to this world and become a lord of the lion-throne.
Ten cows with one bull are traditionally known as "the eleven bulls";
having offered these to Śiva, understand now the fruit of that act.
There, possessing an essence equal to eleven, he rejoices happily as he pleases in all the worlds beginning with Śiva, through his various attributes such as power and enjoyment.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures arising from all cities for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
At the end of that, having attained knowledge through the grace of the Supreme Lord,
one is liberated from the thicket of delusion and abides solely within one's own self.
One should give a bull, most beautiful, to Śiva along with a hundred cows;
together with those born of twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one shall hear [the teaching] and obtain its fruit.
By means of innumerable Great Vehicles, which possess the splendor of ten million suns, are endowed with all desirable things, and are honored by gods and asuras;
Possessing the strength of a hundred Rudras like another Vīrabhadra,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva and become the sovereign of all;
having enjoyed vast pleasures until the dissolution of all embodied beings, he shall remain there.
Having cast off the sheath of the body, he shall attain absolute liberation (kaivalya).
He is omniscient, supreme over all, pure, and established in his own self;
he is omnipresent, perfectly complete, and like Śiva, the immutable Lord.
Whoever should give a beautiful cow with both mouths to Śiva shall obtain that same fruit which is gained by giving the earth consisting of the seven continents.
When two feet and half the head of a cow have emerged from the grain exactly as it should be, that cow should be known as the Earth; the giver of such a cow shall be a lord of the earth.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Rule for Giving Gifts," within the section on the Procedure for Fasting in the *Śrī Śivadharmaśāstra*.
Chapter Eleven.
Nandikeśvara said:
For all the social classes (varṇas) who practice the way of life dedicated to Śiva...
The Śivadharma was spoken by Śiva for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a woman, or a Śūdra, or one who has entered the Śiva-āśrama;
whether a forest-dweller, a householder, or anyone else who has entered the Śiva-āśrama.
To the north of his own hermitage, he should construct a very beautiful flower garden,
provided with other buildings, and in the northeast, a temple for Īśvara.
In the absence of a specific location, one should build it on a spot where space is available on the ground;
to the south of Śiva, one should construct a dwelling for those who have come as his devotees.
One should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual with devotion;
or one may worship Śiva with devotion twice or even once a day.

One should never eat without having first worshipped Śiva out of delusion; this is to be known as the supreme dharma. A human being remains subject to the remainder [of his karma] even in cases of the obstruction or interruption of duties, illness, loss of wealth, and so forth.
One should worship with devotion through the mind or through verbal acts such as recitation;
worship should always be performed with diligence by those who have taken refuge at the presence of Śiva.
The yogi should worship with his mind, or with flowers grown in the forest;
for the sake of Śiva, that injury to flowers which occurs is not truly injurious.

Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva’s image and the sacred fire, a devotee of Him who honors the lunar days, and one who avoids sexual intercourse on festival days— he is the illustrious householder in the abode of Śiva.
One should cook for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, guests, and mendicants, but never for one's own sake alone.
He who cooks out of delusion for his own gratification lives for the sake of hell.
For those whose cooking is for the sake of the gods and whose sexual union is for the sake of progeny, [their life is well-lived].
Their life is for the sake of heaven; in the opposite case, it is for the sake of hell.
One should perform the worship of Śiva with one-third of one's wealth, or even with half of that; for life itself is not permanent.
One should acquire wealth through righteous means and avoid unrighteous ways;
he who lives by means of wealth not honored through righteousness lives for the sake of hell.
He who is a celibate student of Śiva should be devoted to the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire.
One who has conquered the senses, is peaceful, and is either a naiṣṭhika or a bhautika,

being liberated from all attachments and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits— such a person dwelling in the forest, devoted to the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire, is to be known as a Śiva-vaikhānasa.
One who has emerged from all attachments, who is always devoted to the meditation on Śiva,
who is established in the sacred ash, and whose senses are conquered— such a one is to be known as a Śivayati.
He should hold a multitude of rudrākṣa beads in his hands and wear a single matted lock on his head;
for those residing in the hermitage of Śiva, there should be a liṅga and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with sacred ash.
Whoever wears a rudrākṣa on the hand, the head, or as a sacred thread (upavīta),
goes upward above all beings and proceeds to the world of Rudra.
Those devoted to Rudra should always wear a single lock of matted hair on their heads;
it destroys wicked beings, and in that way, one attains the state of Rudra.

He who applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Śiva. The strength and potency of the fire of Rudra is what is proclaimed as these ashes.
It is the destruction of all the wicked and the purification of all sins;
it is the yogi’s bath for every limb, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
One who, with senses restrained, performs the fire-related bath daily at the three junctions of the day shall constantly practice and swiftly attain the yoga of the Self.
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall go to the supreme goal;
the bath of ashes possesses innumerable times more merit than the bath of water.
Therefore, having abandoned the Varuna bath, one should perform the Agneya bath;
by performing the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), one obtains all the merit found in all sacred fords and the fruit of all sacrifices.
Whether one is burdened by great sins or even by all possible transgressions,
there exists no purifier more supreme than bathing with sacred ash.
Having spoken thus to the sages and the gods, Lord Śiva himself bathed;
from that time forward, Brahmā and the others, as well as the sages, have sought Śiva.
Everyone, with great effort, performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) in its entirety;
therefore, whoever should perform this Agneya bath of Śiva, [attains the highest state].

With this very body, he is Rudra; there is no doubt about this. Whether one is of bad conduct or endowed with virtue, whoever they may be, [they are so] by those who seek the fruit [of their actions].
One who is endowed with prosperity and authority is worthy of worship like a prince;
for one who honors a worthy recipient of virtue, there is the honoring of his command.
Therefore, one should worship the teaching without hesitation through the command of Śiva;
by worshipping the command of Śiva, Śiva himself is directly worshipped.
Therefore, one with a non-conceptual mind should worship the teaching of Śiva;
for even he who wears the divine ashes as an outward disguise attains that goal which cannot be reached even by hundreds of Vedic sacrifices.
Having become free from all stains by means of the ritual for sipping water (ācamana) and with the auspicious ashes (śivabhasman),
one should always touch water with the mouth for the sake of purifying any lingering scent or residue.
For even one devoid of perfumes and ointments is purified by purity of intention;
for one whose intention is pure, there is purification through the purity of being, and from that, a state of pure being arises.
[The sixfold bath consists of: the watery, the fiery, the divine, the windy, and the mental.
Five types of baths have been prescribed for Brahmins for the sake of purification:
the Vāruṇa bath, the Āgneya bath which is performed with ashes, and so forth.
By means of rain accompanied by sunshine, the divine [purification] is through the wind, and that of cattle is through dust;
the mental [purification], consisting of meditation, mantras, and so forth, was ordained by the Source of the Universe.
With a thousand water-pots and a hundred loads of earth.
One who practices purification until death is not purified if the mind is corrupt.
One's desire should be purified by one's disposition; one should drink water that has been filtered through a cloth.
One should place one's foot purified by vision; one should speak words purified by truth.
One should carry a bundle of water, and there should be a sifting of food at the beginning of each fortnight.
Just as there is merit in initiation, that same merit shall arise from the practice of breath-control (pavana),
whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, subsisting on alms and free from desire.
A mendicant should be silent, compassionate toward all beings, and possess a tranquil mind;
he should practice alms-gathering like a bee and avoid food from a single house. It is traditionally taught that for householders, alms-food from a single house is equal to fasting.
Even a Śūdra who is liberated from all attachments and devoted solely to Śiva shall, by performing the tonsure ceremony here, become an attendant of the lords of yogins.
That community, devoted to the dharma of Śiva, shall dwell eternally in that monastery;
its sole activity shall be the cultivation of flower gardens, and it shall be intent on the practice of tending those flowers.
Constantly engaged in the threefold practice of bathing, ritual worship, and wearing a loincloth,
one shall attain the station of Yoga through the yoga of devotion to the yogis. Those who are peaceful, intent on meditation upon Śiva, and devoted solely to the worship of Śiva [attain the same].
These people, purified in their inner being, have taken refuge in the hermitage of Śiva;
they must observe the eight great vows (mahāvrata) prescribed by the Lord for those seeking Śiva.
Among all vows, the supreme dharma is fulfilled in this:
devotion to Śiva, constant forbearance, non-violence, and perpetual tranquility.
Contentment, truthfulness, non-stealing, and celibacy as the eighth;
[these are practiced] through actions, mind, and speech with worship according to one's capacity.
Devotion to Śiva should always be practiced, and likewise toward the yogis of Śiva;
one should protect the devotees of Śiva no differently than one's own body.
One should perform what is pleasing for them [the devotees] to protect them from fear, poverty, suffering, and diseases.
What can be done by men for Śiva, who is already perfect?
Whatever is done for the sake of the devotees of Śiva is truly done for Śiva himself.
One must travel even a very great distance to where the devotees of Maheśvara reside; they are to be propitiated with diligent effort, for Hara is ever present in their company.
He who is a devotee of Maheśvara and is always intent on the worship of Śiva,
having carried out his command according to the rule, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
he is constantly devoted to the stories of Śiva and eternally dedicated to Śiva.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one shall attain the status of Gaṇapati.
One should worship with devotion a devotee of Śiva who has come to a Śiva hermitage.
He who offers a welcome, a prostration, or a respectful greeting, along with a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, the honey-mixture, and other foods;
He who personally offers a seat to a devotee of Śiva who has arrived is honored in the world of Agni for ten thousand years.
One shall dwell for twenty thousand years in the city of Indra by devoutly washing the feet of a peaceful devotee of Śiva.

Then, having offered an anointing of clarified butter, that man is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu (the man shall dwell in that world). To a devotee of Śiva who has arrived, he who offers the respectful oblation (arghya) with devotion, preceded by water for the feet and water for sipping, goes to the world of the Sun.

Having received a twice-born who is a devotee of Śiva and having fed him according to the prescribed rule with the offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
By massaging one who is weary, one is honored in the world of Soma;
by providing shelter, one shall obtain a golden house in heaven.
By giving very cool water, one shall obtain all desires;
by the gift of a lamp, one shall attain the eye of knowledge that transcends the senses.
By the gift of a soft bed, one becomes a lord of the lion-throne;
he who gives a bath with water shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
One who fans with a palm-leaf fan a traveler whose limbs are covered in beads of sweat and who is emaciated by fatigue,
is honored in the world of Vāyu.
By protecting one who is afflicted by hunger and thirst, one who is exhausted, one who is soiled, or one who is diseased,
according to one's ability, one is liberated from all sins.
Having diligently brought about the welfare of one afflicted by disease through medicines and other means,
one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas.
Sunk in an ocean of great suffering, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and deprived of consciousness.

Having extracted [the essence] according to one's ability, one shall attain all desires. Out of compassion for all beings, food should be given according to one's own capacity even to those who are fallen, the accused, those of mixed caste, dogs, caṇḍālas, and birds.
Even a very small gift, when given out of compassion, becomes inexhaustible;
therefore, among all beings, the gift of compassion is supreme.
In the absence [of these], one who gives grass, ground, water, vessels, fuel, fruit,
and so forth to people who have arrived— whether out of love or even without affection— attains heaven.
Indeed, pleasant speech in this world is like a staircase to heaven;
for those whose words are always sweet, there is happiness both here and hereafter. Their speech flows with nectar and is as cool to the touch as sandalwood.
Having spoken words that do not contradict the Dharma, one shall attain imperishable happiness.
O best of Brahmins, enough with giving, or with sacrificing and studying!
This pure and pleasing speech of yours is a staircase to heaven.
Rising to meet someone, approaching them, following behind them, speaking kindly,
and being the first to speak— seeing these qualities in each individual are causes for rebirth in heaven.
One should inquire with devotion of a visitor who has arrived, "Welcome," and with humility;
and upon his departure, one should say, "May your paths be auspicious."
"May there be eternal auspiciousness for you, which accomplishes all goals without exception. This blessing should always be uttered in all undertakings.
In discourses beginning with salutations, in the recitation of blessings and auspiciousness, and in all ritual acts, one should always say: "May it be well for you."
Practicing such conduct of Śiva, the follower of the Śiva-āśrama,
being liberated from all sins without exception, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whatever devotion is always offered by men toward the devotees of Śiva,
that devotion is eternally offered to Śiva himself by those practitioners.
When reviled or even beaten, he who does not revile in return nor strike back— remaining composed, with speech and other faculties undisturbed— is said to possess true patience.
Of all sacred fords, the ford that reaches the further shore of knowledge is supreme;
there is no ford higher than the ford of knowledge, which is filled with the water of forbearance.
Knowledge, yoga, austerity, recitation, and virtuous acts such as sacrifice and charity—
Since anger is for one who is wrathful in vain, one should therefore abandon anger.
Unpleasant speech burns the vital points, the bones, the life-force, and the heart;
therefore, one should not speak what is unpleasant, especially toward a devotee of Śiva.
Forgiveness is the gift, forgiveness is truth, forgiveness is non-violence, and forgiveness is sacred learning;
forgiveness is heaven and liberation—forgiveness sustains this entire world.
He is a hero, courageous, wise, an ascetic, and one who has conquered his senses—
those who cannot endure even an arrow, for they have been torn apart by the enemy that is anger.
Having reached the world with the stainless and cooling waters of patience,
one attains happiness in this life and a blissful state in the next.
He who always acts in every way for the welfare and well-being of all beings as he does for himself— this is declared to be non-violence.
Whatever fruit one obtains by knowing all the scriptures and the Vedas,
the merit of one who does not harm living beings is even greater than that.
Even one who might give away the entire three worlds filled with jewels,
or perform all forms of austerity, would be equal to that through non-violence alone.
The supreme dharma known as non-violence is proclaimed for those who are capable;
for those who are incapable, this dharma consists of giving, sacrifice, and so forth.
We do not perceive anything superior to this gift anywhere in any scripture;
for by the granting of fearlessness to men, this gift is of wondrous appearance.
Having given that which consists of all beings, he who should conduct himself with a peaceful mind finds no fear from any beings in this very world.
He who does not harm living beings, whether stationary or moving,
being liberated from all suffering, shall attain supreme peace.
For those extremely cruel kings who conduct themselves with wicked speech,
they shall be cooked in hells until the dissolution of all beings.
That king who prevents slaughter within his own country rejoices for a long time in prosperity along with his very body.
And at the end of the body, together with his entire family, he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred times ten million kalpas, enjoying great pleasures.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one endowed with all the senses should not engage in what ought not to be done; that, they say, is the characteristic of tranquility (śama).
He whose collection of sense-faculties is ever perfectly stilled, who is peaceful, attains with a tranquil mind the state of Śiva, which is as pure as the rays of the moon.
Contentment is proclaimed as that satisfaction which arises from what is obtained at the proper time, through righteous conduct, by lawful means, and for a necessary purpose.

Regarding objects of the past, the future, and the present, there is always neither attachment nor even recollection; this is what is known by the wise as contentment. By that, all sacrifices have been offered, and by that, that supreme state has been attained.
By whom the house of craving has been abandoned and contentment correctly relied upon.
The happiness that belongs to those of peaceful mind who possess the sovereignty of contentment—
that happiness is not found even in a dream by gods, asuras, or humans.
When one who has personally experienced or seen something does not conceal that matter when questioned,
this speaking of things exactly as they are is the definition of truth;
it is speech that is auspicious and entirely free from causing harm to others.
The merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
truth was shown by its qualities to be superior to ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Knowledge is established in truth; the Dharma is established in truth;
purity is established in truth; liberation is established in truth.
Purity is established in truth; liberation is established in truth.
The taking of another's property from those who are being protected by their master or from those who have abandoned it through negligence— this is the definition of non-stealing.
He who, through non-attachment, does not set his mind even slightly upon the property of others—
whether by deed, thought, or word— that satisfied person shall attain the state of Śiva.
The non-practice of sexual intercourse is that which is without thought and without speech.
The characteristic of the holy life (brahmacarya) is the restraint of all the sense faculties;
truth is established in the holy life, and austerity is established in the holy life.
Knowledge is established in celibacy; forbearance is established in celibacy.
Those who abide by celibacy are eternally established in Śiva.
The destination attained by a celibate student who has stayed for even a single night cannot be reached by a householder, even through hundreds of sacrifices.
Having renounced sexual intercourse even when it occurs, they dwell with minds free from agitation.
"Oh, how excellent is this glorious one who has undertaken great asceticism—
he who avoids sexual union on sacred days and abstains from the wives of others."

He who performs all his actions for the sake of Śiva, the sacred fire, guests, and teachers should be known as equal to a celibate student (brahmacārī), even though he has entered the stage of life dedicated to Śiva.
This triad of stages of life is also to be understood as belonging to the non-violent person;
having completed them, a man is always fit for the service of his teacher’s work.
His undertakings, even those conceived by the mind, are accomplished;
this is the glorious tree of Dharma, born of Śiva, whose branches had been lost.
It is not possible to describe it in detail according to the divisions of the secondary branches;
those who are devoted to Śiva read this supreme chapter on conduct.
Together with those born of their three-times-seven lineages, they go to the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Śivadharmaśāstra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Nandikeśvara said: Now, out of compassion for the devotees of Śiva, I shall speak in brief.
The first [part] concerns the meaning of the branches and sub-branches, which arises from devotion to Śiva.

If, while traveling somewhere, one sees a Śiva-liṅga that has not been worshipped, he who then worships it before proceeding is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. He should take for himself the bath-water, the food offerings, the garments, and other such pleasing things.
It is evident that the fruit which results from taking [the gift] is for the sake of Śiva.
Having seen [these], having reached a sacred place (yātanam), and having paid homage to Śiva, one should proceed;
likewise to a crossroads, a river, a mountain, and a Śiva-yogin.
Having descended, paid homage, and beheld the Linga while observing his vows,
the Śiva-yogin [should descend] from the elephant-vehicle, the seat, and the horse for the sake of the ascetics.
One should avoid deer, camels, poultry, fish, meat, garlic, leeks, onions, and the products of the menstrual period, as well as all things that are contemptible.
By abstaining from fish and meat, one effortlessly obtains the fruit of all forms of generosity, fierce austerities, and ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Out of devotion to Śiva, one should not drink liquor, which is the abode of all defects. Where is liquor and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is meat and where is the worship of Śiva?
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—
all that merit he obtains who completely abstains from liquor.
A devotee of Śiva should avoid food that has been touched by women in their menses, as well as all ritual preparations from conception until the end at the cremation ground.
One should not touch with the foot the shadow of a cow, a Brahmin, ashes, fire, or a linga;
one should not step over flower offerings (nirmālya), nor stand upon impure things, nor remain naked.
One should ward off the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva with devotion; one must not eat them out of greed.
By eating them, or by transgressing that rule, a person of deluded intellect goes to hell.
Śaṅkara does not accept his bathing water, offerings, and so forth;
one who eats filth should never worship Śiva with food offerings or floral remains.
Just as someone would not occupy a plot of ground adorned with their own bodily excrement, so Rudra does not resort to a man adorned with the remains of offerings.
Therefore, a man defiled by the remains of offerings (nirmālya) must not touch the liṅga;
he who swallows the bodily impurity of another shall himself become untouchable.
Śaṅkara does not accept that bath and other rites which are performed with devotion using offerings, remains of flowers, or jars that have been mixed together.
One should avoid disparaging the eight forms of Śiva,
as well as the guru, devotees of Śiva, kings, virtuous men, and ascetics.
On all the eighth days and so forth, during both fortnights of the two months,
one should avoid the work of a mother-in-law, the application of collyrium, anointing with oil, sexual intercourse, and other such acts.
One should perform worship especially with distinction and observe the night-vow (nakta) on this occasion;
one should diligently avoid women, Śūdras, fish, meat, and the like on the sacred festival days (parvan).
One should perform the daily bath either three times a day or at one time;
one should also perform purification with earth and water to remove the clinging of odors.
He who eats food while remaining impure eats nothing but sin.
Therefore, having bathed with either ashes or water, one should eat.
Having bathed in the morning with water or with ashes, one shall go to the auspicious state;
he who, devoted to Śiva, the fire, and the Guru, performs the rites at the three junctions of the day, [attains that state].
Having cast the fire, one should uplift seven times three families;
every four months, one should perform the commencement of a great worship.
One should provide food for the devotees of Śiva and arrange for gifts according to one's capacity;
by performing the Cāturmāsya vow, one shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva, endowed with all sovereign powers and accompanied by twenty-one generations of one’s lineage.
On festive occasions for the gods, during ancestral rites (śrāddha), and on auspicious days,
one should worship Śiva with food offerings and then feed a Śiva-yogin.
The sages and all the ancestors abide by taking refuge in Śiva;
when Śiva is pleased, they all become well-pleased, without a doubt.
One should feed at Śrāddha ceremonies a Śiva-yogin who is covered with wisdom and dispassion, who is devoted to the sacred ashes, whose senses are conquered, and whose mind is tranquil.
If there is a thorough understanding of principles such as Īśvara through discernment, [then that is true knowledge].
The definition of that knowledge is established through its similarity and its difference:
he does not hate what is undesirable when it has arrived, nor does he rejoice in what is desirable;
through detachment, he transcends joy, sorrow, and dejection.
The fruit that belongs to one established in the perfection of Dharma cannot be attained even in a single day.
Therefore, it is not possible for a householder to attain [this state] even in hundreds of eons,
unless he has his senses under control, is serene in soul, and neither hates nor desires.
He who has conquered his senses should be known as one who enjoys objects such as sound and other sense-objects;
endowed with knowledge and dispassion, he is Śiva through his tranquil mind.
A Śiva-yogin is proclaimed as one who is disciplined in the yoga of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-yoga).
From the dharma of Śiva arises knowledge; from knowledge arises the birth of dispassion (vairāgya).
For one endowed with knowledge and dispassion, Śiva-yoga proceeds;
and from Śiva-yoga, he becomes omniscient, perfectly complete, and supremely blissful.
Among all beings, men of the three twice-born castes are the most excellent;
among men, the best of the twice-born are superior; and among the twice-born, those who have mastered the scriptures are the most excellent.
Those who contemplate subtle meanings are to be distinguished from those who merely know the texts;
and among those who know the meaning, the one awakened to the manifold meanings is superior.
Yogis are remembered as superior to ten million who know various subjects;
the sovereign of Śiva-yogis is superior to ten million times ten million yogis.
The yogis who possess knowledge, those perfected in yoga, and the ancestors born of yoga [are likewise distinguished].
When they have eaten, they are satisfied; therefore, such a person is distinguished by the yogis of Śiva.
Whatever fruit is obtained through the performance of all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts, as well as through those things already given—all that fruit one obtains by fully honoring a Śiva-yogin.
The five fires, the sacrificial materials, time, the self, the sacrificial fees, the oblations, and the officiating priests—
through their conjunction with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, this is proclaimed as the Vedic sacrifice.
Celibacy, recitation, silence, forbearance, and moderation in food—
this is the form of austerity, most formidable and characterized by these five traits.
Whatever is desired, whatever is excellent, and whatever may be rightfully obtained—all that should be given to one possessed of virtue; this is the definition of giving.
One should give land abounding in thousands of nivartanas, productive of all kinds of crops and endowed with water; that is called the gift of land.
Having brought the earth under a single umbrella, one should bestow it upon the twice-born;
when this is done on the full moon day by some brahmin, that is called the gift of the earth.
One should give a maiden, adorned and endowed with virtuous qualities, to a twice-born sacrificer who is learned in the Vedas; that is called the gift of a daughter (kanyādāna).
One should give a young cow that is free from all defects, well-nourished, and purified by yoga; this is declared to be the gift of a cow (godāna).
Whoever should give new, unwashed garments that are of middling or superior quality;
This, in brief, should be known as the characteristic of the gift of clothing.
A celibate practitioner, established in meditative concentration, tranquil, and devoted to moral discipline,
should not eat during the day or night; this is the characteristic of fasting.
Two hundred and forty morsels of food,
taken according to one's desire over the course of a month, is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
The water resorted to by sages who know all the scriptures, who are devoted to austerity, and whose senses are conquered, as well as by the gods— that is called a *tīrtha* on earth.
One should point out the holy fields that are the abodes of Rudra’s incarnations;
for embodied beings who die in those auspicious fields, the state of Rudra is attained.
He who constructs charitable gifts, guest-houses, wells, gardens,
and temples at sacred fords shall obtain inexhaustible fruit.
Patience, longing [for the good], compassion, truthfulness, generosity, moral conduct, austerity, and learning—
these eight are declared to be the supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient.
Sacrifices, fasts, gifts, austerities, and the fruits of visiting sacred fords [are likewise attained].
Having fully honored a Śiva-yogin, one obtains complete devotion.
Devotion to Śiva, forbearance, truthfulness, complete restraint of the senses,
and friendliness toward all beings— these are the characteristics of the dharma of Śiva.
The Śiva-yogin, the knower of Śiva-knowledge, and he who is devoted to the dharma of Śiva—
these three should be known as the characteristics of a worthy recipient (pātra) of Śiva.
Wealth belonging to a devotee of the Lord should be given for the sake of Śiva, without regard for any other quality; this is the defining characteristic of a gift to Śiva.

He who feeds an excellent twice-born devotee of Śiva at śrāddha ceremonies and other rites uplifts a hundred generations of his lineage and is glorified in the world of Śiva. What need is there for much speaking on this matter? One should simply feed a devotee of Śiva.
Whatever is eaten by a devotee of Śiva is eaten directly by Śiva himself;
it yields the same fruit as feeding ten million twice-born brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.
Giving alms-food to a self-controlled monk who is free from passion is equal to that.
Therefore, with particular faith on auspicious days,
one should feed the best of Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva, dedicating the act to Śiva.
Whether unrestrained or restrained, or even in whatever state he may be,
whoever is a devotee of Śiva is an excellent vessel, equal to Śiva himself.
Indeed, even he who worships Rudra out of mere association or greed for wealth attains a destination that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices;
therefore, he is to be saluted, worshipped, and protected at all times.
Even one who is devoted to Śiva for but a moment, though only by name—
That great ascetic who has attained perfection is a true yogi; he shall go to Śiva.
The merit gained from a funeral rite (śrāddha) performed in the forest is a hundred times greater than that performed at home.
It should be known that there are ten thousand [seats] in those rivers, and an infinite number in the abode of Śiva.
Having properly offered a soft seat made of *vetra* grass to the ascetic, [one should proceed].
Or even one made of wood or ivory, he shall become a lord of lion-thrones;
having offered a loincloth as a garment to a Śiva-yogin.
Having given a woolen cloak, extensive in size, to a Śiva-yogin, one is honored in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of aeons.
One enjoys the fruit of the gold given for every single hair [of the hide];
the skin of deer, tigers, and other such animals should be ground with sesame paste until it is no longer crushed [into a pulp].
Whoever should give soft, dyed-red cloth to a Śiva-yogin,
for as many hairs as there are on the hides of deer, tigers, and other such animals [given by that person], [he shall receive the same number of rewards].
He who gives sacred objects from water or land to a Śiva-yogin is glorified in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of years.
He who gives away a water-pot equipped with a triple-strap, for the sake of protecting minute creatures, shall dwell in heaven for a hundred thousand years.
By performing great austerities, one shall obtain all that merit;
and one shall receive soft, very smooth clothing, free from any harm to living beings.
By offering these to the Śiva-yogins, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
[these include] vessels made of clay, ashes, bamboo, and gourd.
By offering [food] to Śiva-yogins, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
by offering it with the intent of providing sustenance to one who has been given [the gift], one offers it to a Śiva-yogin.
By offering a yogic belt and a sacred thread to a Śiva-yogin, one shall obtain a divine and delightful city endowed with celestial women and enjoyments.
One shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand pairs of garments;
likewise, one gains merit by eating alms-food made of soft bamboo, bottle-gourd, wood, and so forth.
By offering [these] to the Śiva-yogins, one shall always obtain the fruit of all success;
and he who gives wooden sandals or shoes to a devotee of Śiva [obtains great merit].
He who gives food to a Śiva-yogin, or one who gives a spotted-staffed staff, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand moving horses.
The leader of the army, endowed with the support of his forces,
should give either a palm-leaf fan or a parasol to a practitioner of Śiva-yoga.
He shall enjoy a realm of a hundred yojanas under a single umbrella.
To a Śiva-yogin who has attained excellence by relying on the winds [of breath control],
there shall arise a glorious lord of the earth, the support of his lineage and endowed with virtues—
[he] who would give a great book to one possessed of the knowledge of Śiva.
He is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of yugas;
having returned here, he becomes illustrious, rich in happiness, and one who has mastered the Vedas.
One who possesses all knowledge, speaks the truth, and is equal to Bṛhaspati—
he who is a yogi of Śiva, a knower of Śiva’s wisdom, and devoted to the dharma of Śiva.
Having attained Śiva, one becomes equal in soul and equal in power to all;
this applies to whoever performs or causes to be performed the shaving of the hair of Śiva-yogins.
For a hundred thousand years, he is honored in the world of Śiva, which abounds in great enjoyments.
That one becomes Rudra by the gift of rudrākṣa beads—what wonder is there in that?
With that garland always on his hand, Rudra wanders upon the earth;
for the rudrākṣas are Rudra himself, who always follows after the Rudras.
"Because of the wearing of Rudrākṣas, one becomes Rudra both in this world and in the hereafter.
Thus, in the Sadākara [tīrtha], he wears a garland of Rudrākṣas and Rudras.
By a measure of half of half a hundred [verses], one becomes a Rurudra; of this there is no doubt.
And by chanting the Rudra-mantras, the merit becomes ten million times ten millionfold.
Having placed the Rudrākṣa rosary upon his head or on his sacred thread, whatever one eats, that is eaten by the Rudras themselves; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the wearing of rudrākṣas is always praised,
especially for a Brāhmaṇa who acts for the sake of bestowing grace upon others.
Having given even a mere measure of requisites with little understanding and devotion,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred thousand years by means of great vehicles.
One should construct a comfortable and well-protected dwelling for the Śiva-yogins;
for as long as they remain in the temple of Śiva, one gains especially great merit.
As is Śiva, so is the yogi; as is the yogi, so is Śiva.
Therefore, even a tiny gift given into the vessels of the lords of yogis becomes inexhaustible.
Whatever may be useful at whatever time, that should be given to him with effort; for through these two—usefulness and the act of giving—there is welfare for both.
Having constructed an excellent pavilion for the exposition of the Śivadharmas,
adorned with leaves, flowers, and other ornaments, one should place the seat of the Guru therein.
Having placed the great seat of Śiva’s dharma, adorned with garments, flowers, and other offerings,
in front of that guru, one should then worship both.
One should worship both the teacher who expounds the Śiva-dharma and the reciter, for these two are indeed equal.
Whoever thus speaks of the Śivadharmas according to reason and listens to them,
having obtained long life, knowledge, fame, and happiness, shall go to Śiva at the end.
Thus has this eternal Śiva-dharma been declared to you. Whoever hears this Śiva-dharma of all the devotees of Śiva—
this should be told specifically to those who understand it among all the devotees of Śiva.
Whoever, with devotion, proclaims the Śiva-dharma in the hermitages of Śiva,
or listens to it, or reads it, shall obtain the entire fruit as declared in the scriptures.
Having heard all this dharma explained by the son of Brahmā,
Candrātreya, who was a knower of the essence, [bestowed it] upon one of his own lineage who was a devotee of Śiva.
Having extracted the very essence from the essence, the wise Candrātreya has declared this twelfth chapter of the Dharmaśāstra, which is identical with Śiva.
To whatever extent one practices the Śiva-dharma through another's instruction, to that same extent the merit belongs to that instructor as well; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, dharma cannot be known without instruction, nor can it be performed without such knowledge; consequently, the fruit of these two is equal.
This applies to the instructor and the one who consents, as well as the doer and the one who causes it to be done.
And one who maintains what has been done; these five are declared to have equal fruits.
He who maintains what has been built by another gains merit far exceeding that of the original builder;
for a sanctuary, if left unprotected, would quickly go to ruin.
For lands, gems, elephants, cattle, gold, and other such things as clothing,
the protection of what has already been given is indeed more meritorious than the initial act of giving them.
The merit of the donor is even greater for one who protects what has been given;
for that which is not protected perishes on that very day.
Therefore, one should teach the Dharma and practice it oneself;
one should cause others to perform it, approve of what is done by others, and protect it.
Thus, this fivefold Śivadharma has been proclaimed:
Bhadrācala, Rudrakoṭi, Ravimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa,
Bhadrakarṇa, Suvarṇākṣa, and Dyutimān.
This place of Śiva is renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds.
These eight stages should be known as bringing great prosperity and security for Rudra;
the stages beginning with Bhadra and Cala are the cause for attaining union (sāyujya) with Rudra.
Bhāgalaṇḍa, Anduraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kārañjara, Dāruvana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Sthaleśvara.
This is the Pavitrāṣṭaka, which greatly increases merit;
those who die there go directly to the supreme abode of Śiva.
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Babhru, Kanakala,
Vimaleśvara, Uṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīma as the eighth.

This is known as the "Eightfold Secret," which destroys all sins and liberates one from evil. Having gone to the abode of Śiva on the auspicious mountain (Śrīparvata), the glorious man [attains his goal]; there, at Hariścandra, is Jalpamātra and Īśvara.
Madhyamā, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava—
this is proclaimed as the eightfold secret, which is the most supreme among secrets.
Having delivered all his ancestors, he shall go to the auspicious and peaceful state.
Likewise, [he should visit] Amareśvara, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara,
Pāṣaṇḍa, Daṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhūti, and Bhavāntika.
Lakuṭīśvara is highly renowned, as is the great Pratyātmika;
this group of eight Pratyātmikas is the field of Rudra that fulfills all desires.
There, all who have died go to the supreme abode of Rudra.
This group of eight meritorious acts should be known as the defining characteristics of a sacred field (śivakṣetra):
giving gifts, building a dwelling, digging a well, establishing a garden, and constructing a temple for the deity.
Whoever should perform [these acts] at these sacred fords (tīrthas) shall obtain inexhaustible fruit:
forbearance, freedom from longing, compassion, truthfulness, charity, virtuous conduct, austerity, and sacred learning.
This is declared to be the supreme eightfold characteristic of a worthy recipient (pātra).
Thus, this fivefold Śivadharma has been proclaimed.
Obeisance to you, the Lord Mahākāla, who wears a garland of skulls.
O Caṇḍeśvara, salutations to you, whose head is eternally adorned with the crescent moon, who always delight in the garment of an elephant hide, and who perpetually uphold the dharma of the elephant.
O Lord of gods, wielder of the trident, three-eyed one, sovereign of the thirty [gods],
O Great Soul of the triple form, destroyer of Tripura, homage be to you! You are the Lord of all, omnipresent, the source of all, and omniscient, with faces turned in every direction.
O you who abide everywhere, eternal, and all-pervading—homage be to you!
Salutations to You, who pervade all that is moving and unmoving through the division of gross and subtle; You who are infinite, without beginning, unmanifest, and both manifest and unmanifest.
O infinite, eternal, and perpetual one; O universe, the firm Lord of Umā;
O Śrīkaṇṭha, the throat of all, Nīlakaṇṭha—salutations be unto you!
Salutations to You, whose knowledge consists of wisdom, who abide in that state which transcends knowledge, who are both with parts and without parts, and who are devoid of all divisions.
O Lord of Yoga, who art the ruler of the earth, attainable through yoga, whose self is yoga, and who is born from yoga;
O eternal supreme master of great yoga, salutations be unto you!
Consisting of all splendor, you are the brilliance even of the brilliant; you are the treasury of light, the essence of light, and beyond all light—homage be to you!
O Sadāśiva, salutations to you, who are eternally intent upon the meaning of that single syllable "Om," which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
From half a mora to the supreme half, and beyond that half, the highest of the high;
O Peaceful One, who transcends peace, salutations be to You, the most excellent beyond the supreme!
O Śiva, the peaceful one, who is beyond comparison and beyond naming, you who are like a hundredth part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair— homage be to you!
Ungraspable even by the senses, devoid of all objective entities;
infinite, beginningless, unmanifest, residing within the body yet free from the body;
abiding in the heart of all beings and situated in the ether—to You, I offer salutations!
Ungraspable even by the senses, devoid of all objective entities,
that light is the hidden self, the domain of secrets among secrets.
O you who always dwell in the cave, O you whose range is hidden within the caves;
O you who eternally abide in the cave, salutations to you, the one of hidden meaning!

Salutations to you, the Great God, the High-Souled One, whose supreme illusion encompasses both the high and the low; who possesses great knowledge, who transcends the Supreme, and who is attainable through wisdom.
O you who consist of the single syllable, who possess four divisions, who are adorned with four measures,
who have four parts yet transcend all parts, and who transcend the universe— homage be to you! O Īśāna, Īśvara, Brahmā, Sadāśiva— homage be to you!
May all dharmas lead to desire and liberation through compassion for all beings;
may everyone cross over all difficulties and may everyone behold auspiciousness.
May everyone attain a happy rebirth; may there be auspiciousness for all of you. May everyone attain a happy rebirth; may there be auspiciousness for all of you.
Thus ends the Śiva-vidyā in the *Śrīśivadharmasaṃhitā* proclaimed by Nandī.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Branches and Sub-branches."
The Śivadharmas are completed.
Oṃ, homage to the Guru Śiva. May there be auspiciousness. Homage to the illustrious Śiva.
